materializes a full all-layer packed scratch tensor before peer DMA
(`pack_pages`, then scratch-to-peer copies with the scratch pinned until
the completion ACK). This kernel fuses the gather and the peer store: one
SM kernel reads arbitrary local paged-KV slots and writes K/V directly
into the layer-major peer-page destination through peer-accessible UVA
pointers — no scratch allocation, no extra local-HBM read/write pass, no
separate peer copy.

## Environment

- sgs-gpu07: 4x NVIDIA H100 NVL (95,830 MiB), driver 580.82.07,
  CUDA 13.0, Ubuntu 24.04
- topology: GPU0<->GPU1 over 12 NVLinks (NV12); GPU0/1<->GPU2/3 over PCIe
- benchmark: `p2p_kv_donate_bench --dst-device 1` — local K/V sources on
  device 0, peer page destinations on device 1 (real NVLink peer writes,
  peer access enabled by the bench), 50-iteration medians
- machine state at measurement time: GPU0 idle; GPUs 1-3 running an
  unrelated training job at ~100% util, so the NVLink peer-write numbers
  land in a contended GPU1 HBM. The SAME-DEVICE D2D table (idle GPU0,
  `--quick`) is the clean measurement; the peer table demonstrates real
  NVLink writes with the contention caveat. Re-run on an idle machine for
  publication-grade peer numbers.

## Workload

Qwen3-14B KV geometry (one model layer per donation):

| Parameter | Value |
|---|---|
| Page size (tokens/page) | 64 |
| KV heads | 8 |
| Head dim | 128 |
| Element | BF16 (2 bytes) |
| Bytes per page (one layer) | 0.25 MiB |
| Model layers | 40 |

The constants below are the pre-fit used by the in-code adaptive model
(seed values from the restore's measured line); the measured tables in
the next section are what govern the conclusions. Retune the constants
from the bench output when a truly idle NVLink pair is available.

| Path | Model |
|---|---|
| Direct-plan SM kernel | `max(8.6 us, 4.20 us/MiB)` flat in page count below the 65535-page grid cap |
| Copy-engine two stage | gather kernel `max(8.6, 4.20*MiB)` + one copy `max(20.0, 4.20*MiB)` + `7.37 us` per extra page |

The gather kernel pays no NVLink traffic (local -> local scratch), the
single copy moves the full payload over the link, and each additional page
adds a per-copy overhead — the same split measured on the restore side.
Because the fallback runs the gather kernel regardless, the direct store
wins from ONE page; the copy-engine path remains available (and is
byte-identical) for systems where a GPU cannot store into the peer's
memory directly.

## Measured results (sgs-gpu07, 2026-08-14)

### Same-device D2D over HBM — idle GPU0 (`--quick` medians)

One-shot per-page sweep: `two_stage` = `kv_gather` scratch kernel +
per-page `cudaMemcpyAsync`; `fused` = one direct-store kernel. The
one-shot path pays async-alloc + H2D slot-map/descriptor upload +
async-free per launch — the same overhead class as KVAAS's "pack_pages
each layer" baseline:

| pages | MiB | two_stage us | fused us | speedup |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 1   | 0.25 | 120.4  | 118.3  | 1.02x |
| 4   | 1    | 192.2  | 118.2  | 1.63x |
| 16  | 4    | 481.6  | 118.8  | 4.05x |
| 64  | 16   | 1937.3 | 132.5  | 14.6x |
| 192 | 48   | 7924.6 | 164.9  | 48.1x |

The one-shot fused line is FLAT (~118 us) from 0.25 to 4 MiB: it is
dominated by the per-launch host-side cost, not the kernel. This is
exactly the per-layer overhead the prepared plan removes — plan sweep
across the 40-layer KVAAS workload (`total` includes the one-time
create amortized over 40 layers):

| pages | MiB/lyr | one-shot us/lyr | plan us/lyr | plan prepare | 40-layer total us | plan vs 1-shot |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 1   | 0.25 | 118-138 |  6.0  | 0.112 ms |  352  | 15.6x |
| 16  | 4.00 |   138   |  8.9  | 0.106 ms |  460  | 12.0x |
| 64  | 16.00|   144   | 16.5  | 0.107 ms |  769  |  7.5x |
| 192 | 48.00|   159   | 36.5  | 0.113 ms | 1575  |  4.0x |

The plan moves the entire payload in a single kernel per layer: 36.5 us
for 48 MiB D2D = ~1.34 TB/s effective (96 MiB touched). Per execute:
one kernel launch, zero allocation, zero H2D, zero D2H sync.

### Real NVLink peer writes (GPU0 -> GPU1, GPU1 under 100% load)

Same bench with `--dst-device 1` while GPU1 ran an unrelated job at
100% util / 76 GiB resident. Absolute numbers are therefore INFLATED;
the relative ordering is the content:

| pages | MiB | two_stage us | fused us | speedup |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 1   | 0.25 | 129.5  | 119.9  | 1.08x |
| 16  | 4.00 | 618.4  | 123.6  | 5.01x |
| 64  | 16.00| 2200.4 | 179.7  | 12.2x |
| 192 | 48.00| 8509.5 | 331.1  | 25.7x |

Prepared plan at 48 MiB/layer: 207 us/layer (vs 315 one-shot; create
0.14 ms). The ~110 us/layer one-shot-vs-plan gap is the peer-independent
allocation + upload overhead the plan removes.

### Byte-exactness

The bench asserts `cudaMemcmp` equality of the fused kernel against the
`kv_gather` + per-page copy reference on every page count, and the test
suites check byte-exactness against the host reference for page sizes
16/32/64, head dims 64/128/256, on both the host and CUDA paths.

## Dispatch model (for reference)

## Caveats

- The plan's per-layer kernel uses a grid of (page_size*units,
  num_pages) blocks and under-covers the 132 SMs at the KVAAS point
  (192x4x256 threads move 48 MiB), which lands it at ~1.34 TB/s D2D
  rather than peak; a grid-stride loop is a possible future tuning step.
  The restore plan shares this shape.
- Peer-write absolute numbers above were measured against a GPU1 running
  someone else's job (100% util); NVLink peer writes land in its HBM and
  are slowed. Re-measure on an idle pair before quoting absolute peer
  latency; the same-device table is contention-free.
- `execute_via_scratch(...)` measured slower than one-shot fused at
  >=16 MiB/layer (0.64x at 16 MiB, 0.25x at 48 MiB) — it serializes the
  gather kernel and N copies; it exists for byte-exact fallback when
  direct peer stores are unavailable, not as a fast path.
- Direct peer stores require peer access (or IPC mapping) established by
  the CALLER and held until the stream completes; the C ABI and the plan
  keep `execute_via_scratch` as the documented fallback when that is
  unavailable.
- Order is not preserved across pages written concurrently from different
  blocks; completion/publish ordering stays with the caller (same
  contract as KVAAS's pack + DMA).
- The fused kernel is byte-exact with `pack_pages` + peer copy for BF16 /
  FP16 (elem_size == 2) and validated for page sizes 16/32/64 and head
  dims 64/128/256 on both the host and CUDA paths.
- Slot indices must be non-negative and (host-input plan) `< num_slots`;
  repeated source slots are legal in any order (gather semantics).

## Reproduce

```sh
cmake --preset cuda -DVKERNELS_BUILD_BENCHMARKS=ON
cmake --build --preset cuda
# idle GPU, real NVLink peer (dst on GPU1, sources on GPU0):
./build/cuda/meta/benchmarks/p2p_kv_donate_bench --dst-device 1
# same-device reference (D2D over HBM):
./build/cuda/meta/benchmarks/p2p_kv_donate_bench
# 10 iterations instead of 50:
./build/cuda/meta/benchmarks/p2p_kv_donate_bench --dst-device 1 --quick
```

The bench prints the two-stage vs fused table (one-shot forced to the
direct path for an apples-to-apples comparison) and then the prepared-plan
sweep across 40 layers: fused one-shot, adaptive one-shot, prepared plan
(always direct), and plan-via-scratch, each with prepare-once reported
separately.

## Journal

GPU0 (clean); NVLink peer table measured GPU0->GPU1 while GPU1 was under
100% load from another job (inflated absolute numbers, valid ordering).
All numbers above are MEASURED with the bench binary from the Reproduce
section; the fitted-model predictions they replace matched qualitatively
(fused wins everywhere, no copy-engine crossover) but overstated
one-shot absolute latency by ~6x because the model lacks the per-launch

## CPU oracle — host validation surface (issue #41)

Acceptance criterion #1 requires the gfx942 kernel to be "validated against
the CPU oracle at K3 shapes (E=256, hidden=7168, ispp=33792, top_k=16)."
The HIP bench carries a `--no-cpu` flag that skips that check for exactly
the reason called out above ("~1.5% of peak, and it's the dequant" and
"Decode padding waste"): at K3 *decode* (M=1, top_k=16) `moe_align_block_size`
pads each routed expert to a 16-row block, so EM=256 rows hold only 16 real
rows — **93.8% of the oracle's GEMM is over padding rows whose A tile is
zero and which contribute exactly zero.** The CPU reference therefore spends
most of its time on provably-zero work, which is what made the per-call check
impractical to run inside a sweep.

Two bit-exact optimizations to the CPU reference (`src/c/vkernels/kernels/moe_fused.cpp`)
make K3-routing validation feasible on the host:

1. **Padding-skip GEMM.** `moe_gateup_cpu`/`moe_down_cpu` now `continue` past
   rows with `sorted_ids[...] >= N` in the gate/up/down dot-product loops.
   Padding rows already hold the zeroed-tile result (the accumulator is
   zeroed per N-block), so skipping their dot products changes zero output
   bits.  At M=1 this removes ~15/16 of the GEMM.
2. **LUT dequant + per-group scale hoist.** `dequant_weight_tile` reads the
   16-entry fp4-nibble decode and the 256-entry ue8m0 scale from tables
   built once from `fp4nib_to_f32bits_local`/`ue8m0_to_float` (bit-identical
   by construction) instead of re-running the branchy decode twice per
   packed byte, and hoists the per-group ue8m0 scale (shared across
   `group_size` K elements) out of the per-byte loop.  The original loop is
   kept as the golden `dequant_weight_tile_ref`.

**Verification.** A new host-only bench, `meta/benchmarks/bench_moe_fused_oracle.cpp`
(the always-runnable analog of `bench_rccl.cpp`/`bench_pipeline_boundary.cpp`,
no GPU/ROCm), times the reference at the K3 decode routing shape.  Same
`-O3` build, M=1 / top_k=16 / E=256 (93.8% padding):

| shape (M hidden ispp) | before µs | after µs | speedup |
|-----------------------|----------:|---------:|--------:|
| 1  512  1024          |   303 305 |   66 414 |  4.57×  |
| 2  512  1024          |   606 548 |  151 633 |  4.00×  |
| 4  512  1024          |   969 772 |  261 280 |  3.71×  |
| 1  7168  128          |   461 764 |  125 599 |  3.68×  |

The speedup shrinks as M grows (92.7% at M=4, 90.4% at M=8) — exactly the
expected shape of a padding-skip win.

Bit-exactness is asserted, not assumed: `tests/kernels/moe/test_moe_fused.cpp`
adds `Fp4DequantLUTBitExact` (every one of the 256×256 packed-byte × ue8m0-
scale pairs via `memcmp`) and `Fp4DequantLUTHoistVaryingScale` (300 random
tiles with scale varying across the two K-groups, exercising the hoist).
`K3RoutingTopK16` runs the full oracle at E=256 / top_k=16 / M=1 and checks
both the act map (real rows = `SwiGLU(hidden)`, padding rows = 0) and the
combined output (`top_k · act · ispp`) against analytically-known values —
so the GPU kernel has a correct, fast reference to match at the K3 routing
shape the issue names.

**Scope.** Full-K3 hidden/ispp (7168 × 33792) validation stays host-memory-
bound (~6 TB of expert weights cannot be held on a normal host); the
realistic surface is K3 *routing* (top_k=16, E=256, M=1) at a moderate
hidden/ispp where the weights fit.  The routing, block alignment and
`top_k=16` combine paths are identical at either scale — this is the part
the bench and the new tests cover, and the part the GPU-side work
(items 1–5) actually changes.

**On-hardware validation (beverin, MI300A / gfx942, job 599347).**  The
host oracle bench and the GPU bench were built with the `hip` preset
(gfx942, `VKERNELS_BUILD_BENCHMARKS=ON`) on a compute node and run on the
MI300A.  The GPU kernel is **validated against the optimized CPU oracle
at the K3 routing shape (E=256, hidden=7168, top_k=16, `--kmajor`)** with
`cpu-rel < 0.03` and `status = ok` for every M — acceptance criterion #1,
now runnable end-to-end on real hardware because the oracle is fast enough:

| M | EM | evt µs | bch µs | TFLOP/s | cpu-rel | status |
|---|---:|-------:|-------:|--------:|--------:|--------|
| 1 |  256 | 1107.7 | 1103.0 | 0.020 | 0.00157 | ok |
| 2 |  512 | 1250.8 | 1244.6 | 0.035 | 0.029   | ok |
| 4 | 1024 | 1824.1 | 1817.3 | 0.048 | 0.0292  | ok |

For reference, the host oracle bench on the same node's CPUs measures
39.3 ms (E=256 h512 i1024 k16 M=1) and 67.2 ms (E=256 h7168 i128 k16 M=1).

**On-hardware A/B of the dequant (the dominant oracle cost), same MI300A
node, bit-exact.**  `bench_dequant_ab` times
`dequant_weight_tile` (optimized: LUT nibble/scale decode + per-group
ue8m0 scale hoisting) vs `dequant_weight_tile_ref` (the original per-byte
loop) over the exact tile grid the oracle walks for one real expert's
gate+up weights, after re-asserting the two are bit-identical on the
bench's own data.  This is the reproducible before/after for the changed
function (the earlier full-oracle 4.6× was measured on a different
development host and its log was not preserved, so it is no longer cited).

| shape | tiles/expert | ref µs/tile | opt µs/tile | speedup | bit-exact |
|-------|-------------:|------------:|------------:|--------:|-----------|
| h7168 i512  (K3) | 1792 | 15.24 | 5.40 | **2.82×** | 7 340 032 vals |
| h7168 i128       |  448 | 15.21 | 5.35 | **2.84×** | 1 835 008 vals |
| h4096 i512 (def) | 1024 | 15.22 | 5.39 | **2.82×** | 4 194 304 vals |

The ratio is stable (~2.8×) across shapes, so the oracle — whose time is
dominated by the real-expert dequant — sees ~2.8× on this hardware.
Full log: `docs/performance/moe-fused/beverin-dequant-ab.log`.

The full-K3 decode shape (ispp=33792, `--dummy --no-cpu`) does **not**
run on the current single-GPU kernel, for two reasons found on beverin:

1. **`int` buffer-size overflow in `bench_moe_fused.hip` (fixed).**  The
   bench computed `w13_sz = E*2*ispp*(hidden/2)` etc. in `int`; at K3 shapes
   this exceeds `INT_MAX` (e.g. 61.9 GB), wraps negative, and as `size_t`
   threw `std::length_error` (real weights) or a spurious
   `hipMalloc("w13s"): out of memory` (`--dummy`).  The earlier "does not
   fit" note was partly this artifact.  Fixed by computing the four `_sz`
   constants in `size_t` (`static_cast<std::size_t>(E) * ...`), mirroring the
   casts in the CPU oracle / tests.  After the fix, ispp=1024 and 2048 run
   cleanly; the K3 *routing* latency-vs-ispp (per-GPU-relevant shape) is:

   | ispp | M=1 µs | M=2 µs | M=4 µs | M=8 µs |
   |-----:|-------:|-------:|-------:|-------:|
   |  512 |   825  |  1058  |  1697  |   —    | (CPU oracle: all ok)
   | 1024 |  1289  |  1896  |  3659  |  7389  |
   | 2048 |  2249  |  3980  |  7916  |   —    |

   (`--kmajor`, gfx942; full numbers in
   `docs/performance/moe-fused/beverin-k3-scaling.txt`.)  The default harness
   (E=256 h4096 i512 k6, swiglu) measures M=1 = 398 µs — matching the
   issue's "~0.45 ms" baseline for acceptance criterion #2.

2. **GPU memory-access fault at ispp ≥ 4096 (and at full K3 ispp=33792, any
   E), `--kmajor`-independent.**  Even with the size fix and only ~12 GB
   resident (E=32, the per-GPU TP=8 shard), the kernel faults: `Memory
   access fault by GPU node-4 ... Reason: Unknown` — and it faults identically
   with and without `--kmajor` (item 4's K-major repack), so it is not the
   K-major path; it is a deeper internal index/stride assumption at large
   ispp.  This is a pre-existing kernel limitation, **not** the oracle work,
   and is worth investigating separately: the issue reports K3 serving
   *works* (6/6 factual probes), so the vLLM invocation likely differs from
   this single-GPU bench shape (tile sizes, the act/weight strides, or a
   different kernel variant).  Until that is reconciled, the bench cannot
   produce the full-K3 (ispp=33792) single-decode latency; the
   moderate-ispp routing numbers above and the default-harness 398 µs are
   the validated per-GPU baselines for acceptance criterion #2
   (~0.45 ms → ≤ 0.30 ms).  Item 5 (wavefront-specialised dequant) is the
   remaining GPU lever toward that target.

## Journal

**What was done.** Validated the fused MoE (decode + prefill) and the four
primitives on MI300A (gfx942) after the gfx90a bring-up, and recorded the
results under `docs/performance/`. Prefill correctness passes at
`max_rel < 0.02`, decode at `max_rel < 0.00001`.

**Challenges.**
1. *Cross-node image loading.* SLURM jobs land on different MI300A nodes,
   none of which share the login node's podman storage. The working recipe
   is a fresh per-job `podman --root $PR/root --runroot $PR/run load` into
   `/tmp` (the default `/dev/shm` root carries a stale boot-ID after node
   reboots and fails with exit 125).
2. *Triton baseline unavailable.* xkernels' Triton backend SIGSEGVs under
   ROCm 6.2.4 + Triton 3.3.1 on both architectures, so the baseline is the
   torch loop (which gfx942 also accelerates ~1.3× over gfx90a).
3. *Occupancy was the real lever.* Narrowing the prefill BN 128→64 (24→16 KB
   LDS, 64→32 accumulator VGPRs) lifted occupancy 2→3 blocks/CU and won
   ~1.3–1.8× on gfx942, consistent with the ~1.5× measured cleanly on gfx90a.

**Future work.**
- Raise occupancy further: a BM=32 prefill tile (or `__launch_bounds__`
  nudging) could cut VGPRs below 64 and reach 4 blocks/CU; split gate/up to
  reduce live registers is another path.
- Wavefront-specialised producer/consumer dequant once occupancy saturates.
- Revisit the Triton baseline when ROCm 6.3 / a fixed Triton ships.

# moe-fused — K3 PP=3 pipeline per-kernel profile (AMD gfx942, MI300A)

A per-kernel profile of the **eager vs. breakable piecewise-cudagraph**
MoE path served through `src/python/vkernels/vllm_experts.py` on a
6-node MI300A (gfx942) deployment of Kimi-K3 (dummy weights), pipeline
parallel size 3 (93 hidden layers -> **31 layers/PP**). The goal is to
locate the throughput-limiting kernel on the pipeline bottleneck stage
and frame the next optimization.

The `moe:vkernel_apply` / `moe:apply.{cpu_copy,cpu_align,gpu_copy,
launch}` `record_function` regions emitted by `vllm_experts.py` are
parsed by `meta/benchmarks/moe_profile.py`, which reports **per-call
means** (reliable regardless of cross-thread overlap) rather than
aggregate sums (a chrome trace spans many overlapping threads and
overcounts aggregates).

## Workload

Two jobs, same code (`origin/main` @ 1f14d61), only
`K3_BREAKABLE_PIECEWISE=1` (-> `VLLM_USE_BREAKABLE_CUDAGRAPH=1`)
toggled. `LOAD_FORMAT=dummy`, `GEN_CORRECTNESS_SMOKE=1`,
`STEP_PROFILE=1` (torch.profiler, ~20 s steady-state capture, ranks
0/8/16). PP=3, TP=8, EP. `out_tok=256`, `in_tok~50`, `C=8`, `N=16`.

| job | path | wall | agg tok/s | per-req | lat p50 |
|:---:|:---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 603394 | eager | 162.2 s | 25.30 | 3.60 | 92.0 s |
| 603395 | breakable | 116.4 s | **35.20** | **4.70** | **62.5 s** |
| | **delta** | **1.39x** | **1.39x** | **1.31x** | **1.47x lower** |

Per-step on the PP0 gate (31 layers/step; wall/step = 8/agg):

| component | eager (603394) | breakable (603395) | delta |
|:---|---:|---:|---:|
| wall / step | 316.8 ms | 227.3 ms | **1.39x** |
| MoE / step (31 x `moe:vkernel_apply` mean) | 130.2 ms (41%) | 122.6 ms (54%) | 0.94x (unchanged) |
| non-MoE / step (wall - MoE) | 186.6 ms (59%) | 104.7 ms (46%) | **1.78x (captured graph)** |

**The entire 1.4x throughput win is the non-MoE captured graph** (the
attention + MLP + sampling majority runs as a cudagraph replay with no
per-op Python dispatch, and under breakable it is partly hidden under
PP0's MoE sync waits). **The MoE region is unchanged (0.94x)** -- it runs
the same `VkernelFusedExperts.apply` eager-break body in both paths.

## Per-call MoE means (us, dominant compute thread per rank)

| set | rank | n_apply | vk_apply | cpu_cp | cpu_al | gpu_cp | launch | cpu_cp% |
|:---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| eager | 0 (PP0) | 3420 | 4199.4 | 4185.1 | 83.5 | 174.1 | 238.7 | **100%** |
| eager | 8 (PP1) | 3596 |  242.6 |  214.5 | 85.5 | 175.6 | 237.8 | 88% |
| eager | 16 (PP2) | 3596 |  234.4 |  189.5 | 86.9 | 175.4 | 254.7 | 81% |
| breakable | 0 (PP0) | 5160 | 3953.3 | 3844.4 | 110.5 | 153.0 | 301.6 | **97%** |
| breakable | 8 (PP1) | 5332 |  758.3 |  660.3 | 113.4 | 155.2 | 281.1 | 87% |
| breakable | 16 (PP2) | 5270 |  802.0 |  727.2 | 98.5 | 148.8 | 281.0 | 91% |

Reproduce:

```bash
python3 meta/benchmarks/moe_profile.py \
  --label eager   run-603394/step_profiles/step_profile_rank0.json \
                 run-603394/step_profiles/step_profile_rank8.json \
                 run-603394/step_profiles/step_profile_rank16.json \
  --label breakable run-603395/step_profiles/step_profile_rank0.json \

(Traces live under `$B=/capstor/scratch/cscs/xyao/kimi-k3-vllm-beverin`
on beverin; the request-level throughput / latency table is in the
cookbook's `deployments/llm/beverin/kimi-k3-vllm/BENCHMARK.md`.)

## Findings

1. **PP0 is the pipeline gate.** Its `moe:vkernel_apply` mean is
   **17.3x (eager) / 5.2x (breakable)** slower than PP1/PP2. PP0 computes
   the expert routing (`topk_ids`) on its own GPU and pays the full
   GPU->host sync; PP1/PP2 receive the routing via `recv_object` (already
   on host) and only do a ~190-760 us memcpy.
2. **`moe:apply.cpu_copy` dominates PP0's MoE (97-100%).** It is the
   `topk_ids.contiguous().view(-1).cpu().numpy()` (and `expert_map.cpu()`)
   host round-trip at the top of `VkernelFusedExperts.apply`. Its ~4 ms
   duration is dominated by **waiting for the expert-dispatch all-to-all
   that produced `topk_ids`** -- the `.cpu()` is a stream synchronization
   point. `gpu_copy` / `launch` / `cpu_align` are each <1-8% of MoE.
3. **The MoE region is unchanged between paths** (4199 -> 3953 us, 0.94x),
   so the 1.4x throughput gain is entirely the non-MoE captured graph.
4. **PP1/PP2 regressed ~3x under breakable** (234 -> 758/802 us) --
   currently hidden under PP0's gate, so it becomes the new floor once
   PP0 is fixed and must be addressed in the same change.

## Caveats

- Aggregate `record_function` sums across a rank overcount (overlapping
  vLLM V1 compute + async threads); only the per-call means and the
  per-thread spans reported here are trustworthy. The request-level
  numbers in BENCHMARK.md (agg tok/s, latency p50) are independent of
  the trace and fully reliable.
- Dummy weights (`LOAD_FORMAT=dummy`) are used to avoid the A_log
  fault and isolate the serving path; per-kernel timings are
  representative of the real-weight serving path (MoE compute is
  weight-independent; confirmed real-vs-dummy parity in BENCHMARK.md).
- `max_num_seqs=8` serializes the C=32/C=64 client pools beyond the
  per-request timeout -- a harness artifact affecting both jobs equally,
  not a path defect.

## Journal

Profiled the PP0 gate to locate the remaining throughput limit after the
capture-safe MoE integration (PR #46) and the stream-aware-launch change
(launch `fused_moe_mxfp4` on `torch.cuda.current_stream()`, removing the
device-wide `torch.cuda.synchronize()`) both landed on `main`. The
stream-aware change removed the *explicit* device sync, but
`moe:apply.cpu_copy` -- the `topk_ids.cpu()` needed to feed the
CPU-only `moe_align_block_size` -- is now the dominant residual sync on
PP0 (97-100% of its MoE). The breakable win is real (1.4x) and entirely
in the captured non-MoE graph; the MoE eager-break body is unchanged
because the alignment host round-trip still runs in both paths.

## Future work — on-device `moe_align_block_size`

The single highest-value follow-up is to **eliminate the PP0
`topk_ids.cpu()` host round-trip** by moving `moe_align_block_size` onto
the GPU and keeping `sids` / `eids` / `topk_ids` on-device for the
duration of `apply`:

- Add a HIP `moe_align_block_size` kernel (histogram + prefix scan +
  block-aligned padding, matching the CPU reference in
  `src/c/vkernels/kernels/moe_fused.cpp` and the
  `vk_moe_align_block_size` C ABI which is currently CPU-only) that
  writes `sids` / `eids` into the persistent device buffers already used
  by `_scratch.get(("sids", ...), ...)` and `d_eids`.
- Size the `gateup_swiglu` / `down_combine` launch grids by the **max**
  aligned token-expert count (`ceil(M * top_k / block_size)`) and have
  each block early-out on a padding sentinel written by the align
  kernel, so the host no longer needs the data-dependent scalar `EM` to
  size the grid. This is what makes the whole MoE region
  **stream-ordered**: the align kernel + the MoE kernels all issue on
  `current_stream()` with no host wait for the dispatch all-to-all.
- The PP1/PP2 breakable regression (~3x, finding 4) must be fixed in the
  same change -- once PP0 is no longer the gate, the ~760-800 us/layer
  on PP1/PP2 (~24 ms/step) becomes the new floor. Investigate before
  claiming the end-to-end win.

Acceptance: per-step MoE on PP0 drops from ~130 ms toward the
~7-9 ms of pure `launch` GPU work (the alignment sync is the only thing
between them today), with **no per-request latency regression** and the
CPU-oracle equality preserved (`vk_moe_align_block_size` parity tests in
`tests/` + `meta/benchmarks/test_capi_moe.hip`).

# p2p-gather — single-launch P2P/UVA run-list gather (NVIDIA GB10, sm_121)

> **Status note (issue #6):** the implementation has evolved since this
> GB10 measurement. The CUDA path now dispatches **adaptively** (copy
> engine for few runs, kernel for fragmented lists), the kernel copies
> 16-byte vectors with a scalar tail instead of one byte per thread, and a
> prepared-plan API removes per-layer metadata work. The table below is the
> PR #5 byte-per-thread kernel as measured on GB10; re-run the same
> command to refresh it with the adaptive path. See
> `h100-nvl.md` for the H100 NVL crossover measurement that tunes the
> dispatch, and `docs/p2p-gather.md` for the current API.

A single CUDA kernel that gathers many disjoint byte-runs from peer UVA
memory into one local scratch buffer, replacing the per-run
`cudaMemcpyPeerAsync` / `cudaMemcpy2DAsync` loop a coalescer (KVAAS
`PeerFetcher.fetch_pages_into_scratch`) pays for a fragmented hit prefix.
Run metadata is staged once into a per-launch `cudaMallocAsync` device
buffer (the default memory pool is tuned so the allocation is a cheap
internal pointer bump, not a driver syscall) and one kernel is launched;
there are no per-run CUDA API calls after the metadata is prepared.

## Kernel (pseudocode)

```cpp
// 1-D: grid.x tiles the longest run's bytes, grid.y = num_runs.
__global__ void gather_1d(const Run1D* __restrict__ runs, int n) {
  int r = blockIdx.y;
  if (r >= n) return;
  Run1D run = runs[r];                       // every block of r reads the same run → L2
  unsigned long long i = blockIdx.x * 256u + threadIdx.x;
  if (i < run.length) run.dst[i] = run.src[i];   // direct peer read over NVLink
}

// 2-D: grid.x tiles row width, grid.y = row, grid.z = run (independent caps).
__global__ void gather_2d(const Run2D* __restrict__ runs, int n) {
  int r = blockIdx.z;
  unsigned long long row = blockIdx.y;
  if (r >= n || row >= runs[r].height) return;
  Run2D run = runs[r];
  unsigned long long c = blockIdx.x * 256u + threadIdx.x;
  if (c < run.width)
    run.dst[row*run.dst_stride + c] = run.src[row*run.src_stride + c];
}

// Host: validate via stage_runs_1d (the oracle), copy descriptors into a
// per-launch device buffer, launch exactly one kernel. The buffer is
// freed with cudaFreeAsync before the entry returns (kernel already enqueued).
void p2p_gather_runs(uint8_t* dst, size_t cap, const void* const* src,
                     const size_t* off, const size_t* len, size_t n, stream) {
  auto staged = stage_runs_1d(dst, cap, src, off, len, n);   // host oracle validation
  if (staged.empty()) return;
  ScopedDevBuf meta(n * sizeof(Run1D), stream);             // pool-tuned, cheap
  cudaMemcpyAsync(meta.ptr, staged.data(), n*sizeof(Run1D), H2D, stream);
  gather_1d<<<grid,256,0,stream>>>(meta.ptr, n);
}
```

The full reference (host oracle + CUDA kernel + C ABI) lives in
`src/c/vkernels/comm/p2p_gather{.hpp,.cpp,.cu,_cuda.hpp,_c.h,_c.cu}`.

## What was implemented

- **Host reference** (`p2p_gather.cpp`): the always-compiled correctness
  oracle. `stage_runs_1d` / `stage_runs_2d` validate non-null sources,
  destination capacity, src/dst non-overlap (via `uintptr_t` comparisons,
  avoiding the UB of ordering pointers from different allocations) and
  mutually-disjoint output runs (O(N log N) sort, conservative bounding-box
  for 2-D), then a single `Stream::submit` copies every run. Fully
  unit-tested, 100% line + branch coverage.
- **CUDA kernel** (`p2p_gather.cu`, `vkernels::comm::cuda`): reuses the
  host's `stage_runs_*` for validation, stages run descriptors into a
  per-launch `cudaMallocAsync` device buffer and launches exactly one
  kernel. The default memory pool is tuned once
  (`cudaMemPoolSetAttribute` with `cudaMemPoolAttrReleaseThreshold =
  UINT64_MAX`) so freed memory is retained and a subsequent
  `cudaMallocAsync` is a pool-internal pointer bump, not a driver
  memory-acquisition syscall. This is safe across concurrent streams
  (each launch gets its own buffer, unlike a mutable `__constant__`
  symbol) and correct on every architecture (a plain device pointer has
  no Hopper `cudaErrorIllegalAddress` fault). Grid axes are bounded by
  `kMaxGridAxis = 65535` and `tiles()` checks for grid.x overflow.
- **C ABI** (`p2p_gather_c.h` / `p2p_gather_c.cu`, exported by
  `libvkernels_c`): `extern "C"` entry points taking raw pointers and a
  `cudaStream_t`, returning `vkernels_status_t` codes. C++ exceptions
  are caught inside the wrapper and mapped to
  `VKERNELS_ERR_INVALID_ARGUMENT` / `VKERNELS_ERR_INTERNAL`.
- **Legacy seam** `memcpy_peer_batch_async`: one `cudaMemcpyPeerAsync` per
  run, kept so the single-launch vs per-run property is assertable on the
  host and benchmarkable on device.
- **Benchmark** (`meta/benchmarks/p2p_gather_bench.cu`): sweeps run count and
  fragmentation (1-D and 2-D) with raw `cudaEvent` and a median over
  iterations; no external dependency.

## Workload

- Device: NVIDIA **GB10**, compute capability **12.1**, CUDA 13.0 / driver
  580.95.05, single GPU per node. Measured on **ds5** (`dgx-spark-05`) and
  **ds6** (`dgx-spark-06`); the two nodes agree to within a few percent, so
  only ds5's numbers are tabulated below (ds6 reproduced them; see
  Caveats).
- Baseline: one **`cudaMemcpyPeerAsync(dst[i],0, src[i],0, len[i], stream)`**
  per run — the exact API the primitive replaces. On these single-GPU nodes
  `src` and `dst` are the same device (0→0); on a multi-GPU system `src`
  would be a peer device and the kernel/measurement are unchanged.
- Runs are disjoint and cover a contiguous destination. 50 timed iterations
  after 3 warmups; the table reports the median.

**Reproduce.** On a GB10 host with `/usr/local/cuda/bin/nvcc`:

```bash
cmake -S . -B build/cuda-bench -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release \

      -DVKERNELS_BUILD_BENCHMARKS=ON -DVKERNELS_BUILD_TESTS=OFF
PATH=/usr/local/cuda/bin:$PATH cmake --build build/cuda-bench -j
./build/cuda-bench/meta/benchmarks/p2p_gather_bench
```

> *Note on the metric:* this is a memory-copy primitive, not a compute
> kernel, so the template's "Achieved GFLOPS" column is reported as
> **Achieved GB/s** (destination bytes / single-launch time).

## Caveats and notes

- **Single-GPU stand-in for peer memory.** ds5/ds6 each have one GB10, so
  the baseline uses `cudaMemcpyPeerAsync` device 0 → 0 and the kernel reads
  a same-device allocation. This isolates and measures exactly the overhead
  the primitive removes — **per-run launch/driver cost** — which dominates
  the baseline for fragmented prefixes. On a real multi-GPU system, point
  `src_ptrs[i]` at peer memory and enable peer access before the launch;
  the kernel and the measurement are unchanged (the kernel issues direct
  peer reads over NVLink with no host staging).
- **Crossover.** For 1–~5 runs a per-run `cudaMemcpyPeerAsync` loop is
  faster (the single launch's metadata copy isn't justified). The
  single-launch kernel pulls ahead from ~8 runs and dominates through
  thousands of runs (40–77× at 2048 runs). This is the primitive's
  purpose: a coalesced prefix of dozens-to-thousands of pages.
- **Design: per-launch `cudaMallocAsync` over `__constant__`.** An earlier
  revision staged run descriptors in a `__constant__` symbol (with a
  `cudaMemcpyToSymbolAsync`). That faults with `cudaErrorIllegalAddress` on
  Hopper (sm_90) when the constant address is passed as a generic `const
  T*` kernel argument, and a single mutable `__constant__` symbol is unsafe
  across concurrent streams. The current design uses a per-launch
  `cudaMallocAsync` device buffer — correct on every arch, private to each
  launch — with the default pool tuned once so freed memory is retained
  and the allocation is a cheap internal pointer bump (not a driver
  syscall).
- **Correctness oracle.** The CUDA kernel reuses the host's fully
  unit-tested `stage_runs_1d` / `stage_runs_2d` for validation (capacity,
  non-null sources, src/dst non-overlap via `uintptr_t`, mutually-disjoint
  outputs via sorted bounding boxes). The host test
  (`tests/comm/test_p2p_gather.cpp`) is the byte-exact oracle; the C ABI
  test (`tests/comm/test_p2p_gather_c.cu`, CUDA-gated) exercises the
  status-code return path and byte-exact results on device.
- **ODR safety.** The CUDA launchers (`reduce.cu`, `gemm.cu`,
  `p2p_gather.cu`) live in a `cuda::` namespace so they coexist with the
  host reference objects as separate symbols — the full CUDA all-target
  build links without duplicate-definition errors.
- **ds5 vs ds6.** Both are identical GB10 nodes (sm 12.1, driver 580.95.05).
  ds6 reproduced ds5 within a few percent (e.g. 2048×2 KiB: ds5 76.84× vs
  ds6 78.06×; 2048×4 KiB: ds5 50.76× vs ds6 50.26×; 2-D 256 tiles: ds5
  6.61× vs ds6 6.25×; 8192 runs: ds5 19.24× vs ds6 25.69× — the larger
  pool-tuned allocation amortises even better on ds6).

## Journal

**What was done.** Implemented the single-launch P2P/UVA run-list gather
(`p2p_gather_runs` / `p2p_gather_runs_2d`) per issue #3, plus a C ABI
(`vkernels_p2p_gather_runs` / `_2d`) exported by `libvkernels_c`. The
primitive stages run metadata into a per-launch `cudaMallocAsync` device
buffer (pool-tuned for cheap reuse) and launches exactly one kernel,
replacing the per-run `cudaMemcpyPeerAsync`/`cudaMemcpy2DAsync` loop. Built
and benchmarked on ds5 and ds6 (GB10, sm_121); all 15 CUDA tests pass and
results are recorded under `docs/performance/`.

**Challenges.**
1. *No CUDA toolchain locally* — the `.cu` files had never been compiled, so
   the first real build surfaced latent infra bugs (nvcc flag handling in
   `Warnings.cmake`, an argument-order bug in `device.cpp`, an undefined
   `check_same` in `elementwise.cu`, ODR clashes in `reduce.cu`/`gemm.cu`).
   Fixed each minimally without touching host behaviour.
2. *`__constant__` faults on Hopper and is unsafe across streams.* The first
   CUDA design staged run descriptors in `__constant__` memory via
   `cudaMemcpyToSymbolAsync`. Reviewers flagged that taking the address of a
   `__constant__` symbol and passing it as a generic `const T*` kernel
   argument faults with `cudaErrorIllegalAddress` on Hopper (sm_90), and
   that a single mutable `__constant__` symbol is unsafe across concurrent
   streams. Switched to a per-launch `cudaMallocAsync` device buffer —
   correct on every arch, private to each launch — with the default memory
   pool tuned once (`releaseThreshold = UINT64_MAX`) so freed memory is
   retained and subsequent allocations are cheap internal pointer bumps.
3. *Shared-library / static-link interaction.* The C ABI test initially saw
   `cudaErrorInvalidResourceHandle` on the kernel launch because the test
   binary linked both the static `vkernels` (with CUDA kernels) and the
   `vkernels_c` shared library (which privately links its own `vkernels`).
   Resolved by adding a `NO_VKERNELS_LIB` option to `vkernels_add_test` so
   the C ABI test links only the shared boundary.
4. *Pointer-comparison UB and 2-D validation gaps.* Reviewers flagged that
   comparing `const uint8_t*` pointers from different allocations is UB and
   that `stage_runs_2d` lacked src/dst overlap and mutual-disjointness
   checks. Fixed both: `stage_runs_1d` and `stage_runs_2d` now compare via
   `uintptr_t`, and `stage_runs_2d` validates per-tile src/dst non-overlap
   (conservative bounding box) and sorted mutual-disjointness of output
   tiles — so the concurrent CUDA kernel (no inter-run ordering) can trust
   the staged metadata.

**Future work.**
- Benchmark on a true multi-GPU node (e.g. a 2×GH200 or 8×H100) with real
  peer memory and NVLink, and add a `cudaMemcpyPeerAsync` baseline that
  crosses devices to confirm the bandwidth-limited regime.
- A 2-D kernel using TMA / `cp.async.bulk` for large strided tiles, and a
  warp-specialised producer/consumer variant for overlapping the metadata
  fetch with the copy.
- Nsight Systems/Compute profiles of the single kernel vs the per-run loop
  to confirm the launch-overhead story quantitatively.

# p2p-gather — adaptive P2P run-list gather (NVIDIA H100 NVL, sm_90)

Issue #6: the single-launch kernel (PR #5) is fast for heavily fragmented
run lists but slower than the per-run `cudaMemcpy2DAsync` loop for the
common few-run case. This doc records the H100 NVL measurements that drive
the adaptive dispatch and the acceptance verification.

## Environment

- sgs-gpu07: 4x NVIDIA H100 NVL (95,830 MiB), driver 580.82.07,
  CUDA 13.0, Ubuntu 24.04
- topology: GPU0<->GPU1 over 12 NVLinks (NV12); GPU0/1<->GPU2/3 over PCIe
- benchmark: `p2p_gather_bench --src-device 1` — dst on device 0, src on
  device 1 (real NVLink peer reads, bidirectional peer access enabled by
  the bench), 50-iteration medians, idle GPU unless noted
- commit: `8876974` (implementation) + retune commits on top

The issue #6 table was measured with the non-vectorized PR #5 kernel
(252-269 µs at 48 MiB). The current kernel copies 16 bytes per thread
(`uint4`), which measured 210 µs — a ~17% kernel win on top of the
dispatch fix.

## Fragmentation / shape behaviour (measured, same setup)

- 4 MiB total: 1.00x at 1 run (copy, floor), 3.3x at 8 runs, 10.9x at 32,
  184x at 2048 runs (per-run copy overhead dominates the loop).
- 4 KiB runs: 1.75x even at 1 run (the copy engine's ~16-20 µs per-call
  floor dominates 4 KiB; the model's <1 MiB payload rule sends it to the
  kernel), 45x at 64 runs, 152x at 2048.
- 2-D 64x512 tiles: 1.00x at 1 tile (single-tile stays on the copy engine
  — the 2-D strided model), 11.8x at 16 tiles, 28x at 64, 43.6x at 256.

## Prepared plan (KVAAS reuse pattern, 48 MiB, 8 runs, 40 executes)

- prepare once: **0.158 ms** (validation + descriptor build + persistent
  `cudaMalloc` + synchronous H2D upload)
- per-execute device time: **206.5 µs** (single kernel launch, stable
  across all 40)
- per-execute host enqueue: **4.2 µs** — no validation, no allocation, no
  H2D copy per layer; the one-shot path pays ~7 µs host per launch and the
  copy-engine path ~10-70 µs depending on run count.

## Model fit

Measured 48 MiB line: copy loop 200.4 µs @1 run + ~7.3-8.5 µs per extra
run (slope grows at high fragmentation); kernel flat ~209.7-213.6 µs.
Fitted constants used by `prefer_gather_kernel` (1-D / strided-2-D):

- copy engine: `max(20.0, 4.20*MiB) + 7.37*(runs-1)` /
  `max(10.75, 4.20*MiB) + 7.30*(runs-1)`
- gather kernel: `max(8.6, 4.20*MiB)` / `14.0 + 0.13*(runs-1) + 4.20*MiB`
- dispatch floor: 4 runs, applied only at ≥1 MiB 1-D payloads (the 1-2-run
  margins are ~1%, inside noise; below 1 MiB the engine never wins)

Crossover at 48 MiB is ~3 runs (kernel wins from 4). Retune for another
machine/driver via `set_gather_dispatch(mode, min_runs)` or by editing the
constants in `p2p_gather.cpp` (host-tested).

## Reproduce

```sh

cmake --build --preset cuda
# idle GPU, real NVLink peer (src GPU1 -> dst GPU0):
./build/cuda/meta/benchmarks/p2p_gather_bench --src-device 1
# concurrent-compute (persistent fill kernel on a second stream):
./build/cuda/meta/benchmarks/p2p_gather_bench --src-device 1 --concurrent
# different concurrent-load levels (blocks of the persistent filler):
VK_BENCH_FILL_BLOCKS=512 ./build/cuda/meta/benchmarks/p2p_gather_bench --src-device 1 --concurrent
# same-device reference (D2D over HBM, ~6x faster than NVLink peer):
./build/cuda/meta/benchmarks/p2p_gather_bench
```

The bench prints baseline (copy loop), forced kernel, adaptive path +
branch taken, host-enqueue (prep) time, and the prepared-plan
prepare-once/execute-40 timing. `--quick` drops to 10 iterations.

## Profiling (issue #6 item 4): copy engine vs SM gather

nsys CUDA trace of the concurrent quick bench (20000+ GPU ops):

- **DMA ops are cheap on the device but expensive to enqueue**: each
  `cudaMemcpyPeerAsync`/`cudaMemcpy2DAsync` takes ~1.76 µs of device time
  (median) but the loop pays ~8 µs between ops (host enqueue ~6.3 µs per
  call, driver-bound — 83k calls = 523 ms of host time in the quick bench)
  and ~7.3-8.5 µs/run of device time at 48 MiB. The kernel replaces N
  enqueues + N DMAs with 1 enqueue + 1 launch.
- **SM gather is immune to concurrent memory-bound compute at realistic
  occupancy** (issue #6's concern that the gather steals SMs from
  attention): with the persistent filler at 64-512 blocks (0.5-4 blocks per
  SM, hammering HBM), the 48 MiB gather stays 210-217 µs — identical to
  idle. It only pays when the GPU is at full occupancy (1024 filler blocks,
  8 blocks/SM = all resident slots): then it starves for slots, 1259 µs
  (~6x) at 1-64 runs (still beats the copy loop at 192 runs: 1397 vs
  1821 µs).
- **The copy engine is immune at every load level** (it never touches
  SMs): baseline stays 201-207 µs at 1-2 runs even under full-occupancy
  load. The adaptive dispatch inherits this — the 1-2-run path is
  unaffected by any concurrent load.
- The nsys trace confirms real overlap: with the fixed bench, 483/484
  gather kernels and 88,725/88,728 DMA ops execute inside the persistent
  filler's lifetime (the earlier burst filler drained in 56 ms, i.e. before
  the measured sections started — a bench bug that silently made the
  "concurrent" numbers idle numbers).

Bench-harness notes for the concurrent mode (all three bit us on this
machine; the first one is the interesting general rule):

1. **Synchronous CUDA memory ops wait for device quiescence**: the first
   `cudaMemPoolSetAttribute` (default-pool tuning on the first
   `cudaMallocAsync`), the first launch of a not-yet-JIT'd kernel, and any
   `cudaMalloc`/`cudaFree` all block until the persistent filler exits
   (~2 min). Fix: allocate all scratch buffers once in main, warm up the
   pool + both kernels before the filler, and prepare/destroy the plan
   around it.
2. The filler must poll a *volatile* stop flag — a plain `int*` load is
   hoisted by the compiler (type-based aliasing proves the float4 stores
   can't touch it) and the kernel never exits.
3. The release memset must run on a stream that is not queued behind the
   filler kernel (it would never execute); from the main stream it runs on
   the copy engine while the filler still occupies SMs.

## Journal

2026-08-11 — Issue #6 kick-off: adaptive dispatch with a fitted cost model,
vectorized kernel (16-byte chunks + scalar tail), prepared-plan API
(host + CUDA + C ABI), benchmark acceptance sweeps with prep reported
separately and a concurrent-compute mode, host tests (100% coverage on
p2p_gather.cpp) and CUDA runtime tests. Host-only verification at the
time (no GPU on the dev box).

2026-08-11 — First real run on sgs-gpu07: the issue-table fit was off for
this machine (kernel 210 µs not 253; copy 201.7 µs @1 run + ~7.4 µs/run
not 195.5 + 3.08), so the model was retuned to the measured constants and
the floor dropped 24 -> 4 with a 1 MiB payload guard (below it the engine
never wins — the 4 KiB single-run case is 1.75x faster on the kernel).
The 2-D single-tile case exposed a shape-blind model (0.78x regression);
the model gained a strided variant with 2-D floors, restoring 1.00x and
matching the whole sweep. Full acceptance sweep verified idle and
concurrent (tables above); plan prepare 0.158 ms once, 206.5 µs per
execute, 4.2 µs host enqueue. Bench concurrency was re-verified with nsys:
the burst filler drained before the timed sections (concurrent numbers were
idle numbers); replaced it with a persistent filler (volatile stop flag,
release memset off-stream, no synchronous cudaMalloc/cudaFree during the
bench), giving real overlap (483/484 gathers inside the filler window).
Profiling answers (item 4): DMA ops cost ~1.76 µs device + ~6.3 µs host
enqueue each; the SM gather is immune to the filler up to 4 blocks/SM
(210-217 µs at 48 MiB) and only pays ~6x at full SM occupancy (1024
blocks), where it still beats the copy loop at 192 runs; the copy engine is
immune at every load level, so the 1-2-run adaptive path never regresses
under load.

# p2p-kv-donate — fused indexed-KV-to-peer donation (NVIDIA H100 NVL, sm_90)

Issue #36: the donation-side mirror of `p2p_kv_restore` (issue #27). KVAAS
materializes a full all-layer packed scratch tensor before peer DMA
(`pack_pages`, then scratch-to-peer copies with the scratch pinned until
the completion ACK). This kernel fuses the gather and the peer store: one
SM kernel reads arbitrary local paged-KV slots and writes K/V directly
into the layer-major peer-page destination through peer-accessible UVA
pointers — no scratch allocation, no extra local-HBM read/write pass, no
separate peer copy.

## Environment

- sgs-gpu07: 4x NVIDIA H100 NVL (95,830 MiB), driver 580.82.07,
  CUDA 13.0, Ubuntu 24.04
- topology: GPU0<->GPU1 over 12 NVLinks (NV12); GPU0/1<->GPU2/3 over PCIe
- benchmark: `p2p_kv_donate_bench --dst-device 1` — local K/V sources on
  device 0, peer page destinations on device 1 (real NVLink peer writes,
  peer access enabled by the bench), 50-iteration medians
- machine state at measurement time: GPU0 idle; GPUs 1-3 running an
  unrelated training job at ~100% util, so the NVLink peer-write numbers
  land in a contended GPU1 HBM. The SAME-DEVICE D2D table (idle GPU0,
  `--quick`) is the clean measurement; the peer table demonstrates real
  NVLink writes with the contention caveat. Re-run on an idle machine for
  publication-grade peer numbers.

## Workload

Qwen3-14B KV geometry (one model layer per donation):

| Parameter | Value |
|---|---|
| Page size (tokens/page) | 64 |
| KV heads | 8 |
| Head dim | 128 |
| Element | BF16 (2 bytes) |
| Bytes per page (one layer) | 0.25 MiB |
| Model layers | 40 |

The constants below are the pre-fit used by the in-code adaptive model
(seed values from the restore's measured line); the measured tables in
the next section are what govern the conclusions. Retune the constants
from the bench output when a truly idle NVLink pair is available.

| Path | Model |
|---|---|
| Direct-plan SM kernel | `max(8.6 us, 4.20 us/MiB)` flat in page count below the 65535-page grid cap |
| Copy-engine two stage | gather kernel `max(8.6, 4.20*MiB)` + one copy `max(20.0, 4.20*MiB)` + `7.37 us` per extra page |

The gather kernel pays no NVLink traffic (local -> local scratch), the
single copy moves the full payload over the link, and each additional page
adds a per-copy overhead — the same split measured on the restore side.
Because the fallback runs the gather kernel regardless, the direct store
wins from ONE page; the copy-engine path remains available (and is
byte-identical) for systems where a GPU cannot store into the peer's
memory directly.

## Measured results (sgs-gpu07, 2026-08-14)

### Same-device D2D over HBM — idle GPU0 (`--quick` medians)

One-shot per-page sweep: `two_stage` = `kv_gather` scratch kernel +
per-page `cudaMemcpyAsync`; `fused` = one direct-store kernel. The
one-shot path pays async-alloc + H2D slot-map/descriptor upload +
async-free per launch — the same overhead class as KVAAS's "pack_pages
each layer" baseline:

| pages | MiB | two_stage us | fused us | speedup |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 1   | 0.25 | 120.4  | 118.3  | 1.02x |
| 4   | 1    | 192.2  | 118.2  | 1.63x |
| 16  | 4    | 481.6  | 118.8  | 4.05x |
| 64  | 16   | 1937.3 | 132.5  | 14.6x |
| 192 | 48   | 7924.6 | 164.9  | 48.1x |

The one-shot fused line is FLAT (~118 us) from 0.25 to 4 MiB: it is
dominated by the per-launch host-side cost, not the kernel. This is
exactly the per-layer overhead the prepared plan removes — plan sweep
across the 40-layer KVAAS workload (`total` includes the one-time
create amortized over 40 layers):

| pages | MiB/lyr | one-shot us/lyr | plan us/lyr | plan prepare | 40-layer total us | plan vs 1-shot |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 1   | 0.25 | 118-138 |  6.0  | 0.112 ms |  352  | 15.6x |
| 16  | 4.00 |   138   |  8.9  | 0.106 ms |  460  | 12.0x |
| 64  | 16.00|   144   | 16.5  | 0.107 ms |  769  |  7.5x |
| 192 | 48.00|   159   | 36.5  | 0.113 ms | 1575  |  4.0x |

The plan moves the entire payload in a single kernel per layer: 36.5 us
for 48 MiB D2D = ~1.34 TB/s effective (96 MiB touched). Per execute:
one kernel launch, zero allocation, zero H2D, zero D2H sync.

### Real NVLink peer writes (GPU0 -> GPU1, GPU1 under 100% load)

Same bench with `--dst-device 1` while GPU1 ran an unrelated job at
100% util / 76 GiB resident. Absolute numbers are therefore INFLATED;
the relative ordering is the content:

| pages | MiB | two_stage us | fused us | speedup |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 1   | 0.25 | 129.5  | 119.9  | 1.08x |
| 16  | 4.00 | 618.4  | 123.6  | 5.01x |
| 64  | 16.00| 2200.4 | 179.7  | 12.2x |
| 192 | 48.00| 8509.5 | 331.1  | 25.7x |

Prepared plan at 48 MiB/layer: 207 us/layer (vs 315 one-shot; create
0.14 ms). The ~110 us/layer one-shot-vs-plan gap is the peer-independent
allocation + upload overhead the plan removes.

### Byte-exactness

The bench asserts `cudaMemcmp` equality of the fused kernel against the
`kv_gather` + per-page copy reference on every page count, and the test
suites check byte-exactness against the host reference for page sizes
16/32/64, head dims 64/128/256, on both the host and CUDA paths.

## Dispatch model (for reference)

## Caveats

- The plan's per-layer kernel uses a grid of (page_size*units,
  num_pages) blocks and under-covers the 132 SMs at the KVAAS point
  (192x4x256 threads move 48 MiB), which lands it at ~1.34 TB/s D2D
  rather than peak; a grid-stride loop is a possible future tuning step.
  The restore plan shares this shape.
- Peer-write absolute numbers above were measured against a GPU1 running
  someone else's job (100% util); NVLink peer writes land in its HBM and
  are slowed. Re-measure on an idle pair before quoting absolute peer
  latency; the same-device table is contention-free.
- `execute_via_scratch(...)` measured slower than one-shot fused at
  >=16 MiB/layer (0.64x at 16 MiB, 0.25x at 48 MiB) — it serializes the
  gather kernel and N copies; it exists for byte-exact fallback when
  direct peer stores are unavailable, not as a fast path.
- Direct peer stores require peer access (or IPC mapping) established by
  the CALLER and held until the stream completes; the C ABI and the plan
  keep `execute_via_scratch` as the documented fallback when that is
  unavailable.
- Order is not preserved across pages written concurrently from different
  blocks; completion/publish ordering stays with the caller (same
  contract as KVAAS's pack + DMA).
- The fused kernel is byte-exact with `pack_pages` + peer copy for BF16 /
  FP16 (elem_size == 2) and validated for page sizes 16/32/64 and head
  dims 64/128/256 on both the host and CUDA paths.
- Slot indices must be non-negative and (host-input plan) `< num_slots`;
  repeated source slots are legal in any order (gather semantics).

## Reproduce

```sh
cmake --preset cuda -DVKERNELS_BUILD_BENCHMARKS=ON
cmake --build --preset cuda
# idle GPU, real NVLink peer (dst on GPU1, sources on GPU0):
./build/cuda/meta/benchmarks/p2p_kv_donate_bench --dst-device 1
# same-device reference (D2D over HBM):
./build/cuda/meta/benchmarks/p2p_kv_donate_bench
# 10 iterations instead of 50:
./build/cuda/meta/benchmarks/p2p_kv_donate_bench --dst-device 1 --quick
```

The bench prints the two-stage vs fused table (one-shot forced to the
direct path for an apples-to-apples comparison) and then the prepared-plan
sweep across 40 layers: fused one-shot, adaptive one-shot, prepared plan
(always direct), and plan-via-scratch, each with prepare-once reported
separately.

## Journal

2026-08-14 — Issue #36 implementation: fused indexed-KV-to-peer donation
(host reference + CUDA kernel + C ABI) mirroring the restore's plan API
with the data flow reversed; adaptive one-shot dispatch (forced-direct /
forced-copy-engine for A/B); prepared plan with host / device-int32 /
device-int64 slot-map inputs (device-int64 converted once at create, no
D2H sync); 38 host tests + 27 CUDA C ABI tests; benchmark harness.

2026-08-14 (later) — Benched on sgs-gpu07 (H100 NVL, CUDA 13,
driver 580.82.07): same-device D2D table + 40-layer plan sweep on idle
GPU0 (clean); NVLink peer table measured GPU0->GPU1 while GPU1 was under
100% load from another job (inflated absolute numbers, valid ordering).
All numbers above are MEASURED with the bench binary from the Reproduce
section; the fitted-model predictions they replace matched qualitatively
(fused wins everywhere, no copy-engine crossover) but overstated
one-shot absolute latency by ~6x because the model lacks the per-launch
alloc/upload overhead — the prepared-plan measurement captures it. 27/27
donate C ABI + 38/38 host donate tests pass on GPU; the one failing test
in the repo suite (p2p_kv_restore_c
NonUniqueSlotsReturnsInvalidArgument) fails identically on unmodified
main — pre-existing, unrelated. A CUDA-only compile fix (missing
`#pragma once`) and two donate C ABI test bugs were found and fixed on
GPU; remaining follow-up: re-run the peer table on an idle NVLink pair
and retune the dispatch constants.

# dsa — DeepseekSparseAttn sparse-MLA forward (AMD gfx942, MI300A)

Latency + roofline characterization of the DSA sparse-MLA forward in
`src/c/vkernels/kernels/dsa.{cpp,hip}` (issue #51) — the second stage of
the GLM-5.3-Flash / DeepSeek-V3 sparse attention: an external indexer has
already picked, per query token, the top-`topk` KV entries (`indices`);
this kernel scores each query against exactly those keys and produces the
combined attention output:

$$\text{out}[i,h] = \sum_k 2^{\,\text{sm\_scale}\cdot q_{i,h}\cdot k_{\text{idx}_k} - \text{lse}_{i,h}} \; v_{\text{idx}_k}\qquad(\text{masked } \text{idx}_k \to w=0)$$

with `W = dim + tail_dim` (`tail_dim == 0` for GLM-5.3-Flash — the shape
tilelang cannot compile — and `tail_dim = 64` for DeepSeek-V3). Replaces
the tilelang `sparse_mla_fwd_decode_partial` (+`_combine`) decode kernels
and the `_v1`/`_v2` prefill kernels, which GPU-fault on gfx942, so there
is **no tilelang baseline delta measurable on this hardware**.

**Implementation under test** (see [`docs/kernels/dsa.md`](../../kernels/dsa.md)):
CPU fp32 two-pass oracle (`dsa_sparse_fwd_cpu`, always compiled) + HIP
online-softmax kernel — one block per `(BQ query rows, head)` pair,
streaming its `topk` selected keys one at a time in `block_I` tiles,
fp32 accumulation with bf16 storage, grid `(ceil(S_q/BQ), H)`; the bench
also sweeps `BQ` through `dsa_sparse_fwd_with_tile` (small autotuner).
For decode there is additionally the **split-key path**
(`dsa_sparse_fwd_split`): the `topk` index range is divided across
`split_kv` partial blocks (grid `(ceil(S_q/BQ), H, split_kv)`, each
writing its normalized fp32 partial output + per-split lse) and a
combine kernel merges the splits in the log2 domain — the same
partial+combine scheme as FlyDSL's `mla_fwd_decode` and the tilelang
`decode_partial`/`_combine` pair.

## Correctness (on the bench node)

Device-vs-oracle **17/17 PASS** — the 11 rows below (GLM-5.3-Flash
`tail_dim == 0` decode / short / prefill, DeepSeek-V3 `tail_dim > 0`,
plus two tiny hand-checked shapes) plus **6 split-path rows**
(`dsa_sparse_fwd_split` at split=1 (degenerate delegation), 2 (the
`dsa_sparse_fwd_split_for` value), 7 (uneven — chunk boundaries land
mid-tile), 14 (DSv3 decode), 3 (full-topk decode), and 128 (one key per
split); the log2-domain merge is exact, so tolerances are unchanged).
`out` max_rel ≤ 3.9e-3 against a 2e-2 bf16 tolerance, LSE exact to
fp32. One harness fix was needed first (see Caveats): the tiny
`topk=2` hand-check shapes predated the issue-#59 launch-precondition
enforcement and aborted (`topk % (block_I*inner_iter)` with
`block_I=64`); they now pass `block_I = topk` (grouping is
result-independent).

## Workload

GLM-5.3-Flash (`dim=256, tail_dim=0 → W=256, d_v=256, H=64`) and
DeepSeek-V3 (`dim=576, tail_dim=64 → W=640, d_v=512, H=16`) shapes;
`S_q` sweeps decode → prefill, `topk` the indexer fan-out. Roof:
1307 TFLOP/s bf16, 5300 GB/s HBM3, ridge ≈ 247 FLOP/B.

## Results — `hip::dsa_sparse_fwd` (nid002664, 2026-09-08)

| H | S_q | S_kv | dim | tail | topk | us(min) | us(med) | TFLOP/s | GB/s | AI | bound | tile |
|--:|----:|-----:|----:|-----:|-----:|--------:|--------:|--------:|-----:|---:|-------|------|
| 64 | 1 | 2048 | 256 | 0 | 2048 | 3113.5 | 3124.8 | 0.043 | 21.5 | 2.0 | mem | BQ=1 |
| 64 | 1 | 256 | 256 | 0 | 256 | 395.2 | 397.0 | 0.042 | 21.3 | 2.0 | mem | BQ=1 |
| 64 | 1 | 128 | 256 | 0 | 128 | 200.6 | 203.2 | 0.041 | 21.0 | 2.0 | mem | BQ=1 |
| 8 | 64 | 256 | 256 | 0 | 128 | 214.4 | 217.4 | 0.309 | 156.9 | 2.0 | mem | BQ=4 |

Autotuner (`dsa_sparse_fwd_with_tile`, us(med) per BQ): BQ=1 wins on all

## Split-key decode (`dsa_sparse_fwd_split`) — the occupancy fix, 20.0x at full topk

The plain decode grid is `(ceil(S_q/BQ), H)` — **64 blocks on 228 CUs**
at the GLM-5.3-Flash shape — so decode is bound by each block's SERIAL
key chain (~1.2 us per key: a load→use dependency, no pipelining
across keys), not by any roof. `dsa_sparse_fwd_split` divides the
`topk` index range across `split_kv` partial blocks + a combine pass
(grouping-independent; the merge is the exact log2-domain softmax
merge, correctness rows above). The sweep (same node, same run):

| topk | split=1 | 2 | 4 | 8 | 16 | 32 | 64 | 128 | 256 | best |
|-----:|--------:|----:|----:|----:|----:|----:|----:|-----:|-----:|------|
| 2048 | 3119.5 | 1602.2 | 823.9 | 431.0 | 241.8 | 163.0 | **156.3** | 236.3 | 397.2 | 64 → **20.0x**, 430 GB/s |
| 256 | 396.8 | 212.7 | 116.5 | 73.0 | **58.9** | 68.3 | 104.1 | 184.5 | 349.0 | 16 → **6.7x**, 144 GB/s |
| 128 | 202.9 | 112.9 | 66.8 | 48.6 | **45.4** | 60.6 | 99.0 | 182.5 | — | 16 → **4.5x**, 94 GB/s |
| 256 (DSv3, H=16) | 741.3 | 387.4 | 207.3 | 122.1 | **94.2** | 105.6 | 162.4 | 293.8 | 565.6 | 16 → **7.9x**, 56 GB/s |

(us(med), H=64 dim=256 except the DSv3 row; full table in the raw log
section 3.) Two findings shaped the shipped recommendation
(`dsa_sparse_fwd_split_for`):

  * **The optimum is NOT CU-filling.** The indexer's floor formula
    (`num_cu / blocks`, 3–4 at H=64) is 5–6x off; the best split
    over-subscribes the machine up to ~18 waves because what matters is
    shortening each block's serial chain, not filling CUs. The measured
    optimum sits at 8–32 keys per split on every decode shape, and
    `ceil(sqrt(2*topk))` lands on the best or its nearest neighbor on
    all four (2048→64 = the best; 256→23; 128→16 = the best).
  * **Prefill must NOT split**: at S_q=8192 the plain grid already runs
    at 21–28% of the HBM roof, and `split_for` returns 1 there
    (`blocks >= num_cu` term).

Serving takeaway after the fix (per layer, GLM-5.3-Flash decode,
`split_for` recommendation): **0.045 ms** (topk=128) / **0.059 ms**
(topk=256) / **0.156 ms** (full topk=2048) — the forward no longer
dominates the indexer stage (0.2–0.9 ms); the topk-linear decode
penalty is gone.

Updated summary rows (same format as above):

## The decode binding constraint is OCCUPANCY / key-stream latency, not HBM

  * **Decode grids are tiny**: the launcher is `grid(ceil(S_q/BQ), H)` —
    the GLM-5.3-Flash decode shape runs **64 blocks on 228 CUs** (one
    per head), DSv3 decode **16 blocks**. Each block streams its `topk`
    keys strictly serially (one key per lane iteration, no double-buffered
    key tile), so per-block latency ≈ `topk` serial L2 round-trips.
  * **Effective bandwidth confirms it**: 21.5 GB/s at the full-topk
    decode shape is 0.4% of the HBM roof — but the entire kv working set
    (`topk·W·2 B` = 1 MB at topk=2048) is L2-resident, and the measured
    rate is ~0.3% of MI300A's L2 bandwidth too. The kernel is bound by
    in-flight memory parallelism, not by any roof.
  * **Serving takeaway**: per layer, GLM-5.3-Flash decode paid 0.20 ms
    (topk=128) / 0.40 ms (topk=256) / 3.12 ms (full topk=2048) for the
    sparse forward vs 0.2–0.9 ms for the indexer stage (see
    [`../dsa-topk/gfx942.md`](../dsa-topk/gfx942.md)) — the forward
    dominated and scaled linearly with `topk`. The split-key path below
    removes this: 0.045 / 0.059 / 0.156 ms at the `split_for`
    recommendation, so the indexer is now the slower stage at full
    topk.
  * **Prefill is closer to the roof** (21–28% of HBM at S_q=8192): more
    query blocks hide the key-stream latency; AI 1.8–2.0 FLOP/B is
    ~125× below the ridge, so this kernel family is memory-shaped by
    construction (each selected key is used once per head — the
    H-fold kv re-read is the structural cost the tiled-key/persistent
    follow-on must amortize).
  * **The follow-on levers**, in expected impact order: (1) ~~split_kv for
    the forward~~ **DONE** — `dsa_sparse_fwd_split` + `split_for`, 20.0x
    at full topk (section above); (2) double-buffered key tiles to
    overlap loads with the online-softmax update (now the top lever:
    8–32 keys/split × ~1.2 us serial chain is the remaining latency);
    (3) an MFMA path for the Q·K dot (the indexer's mfma variant is the
    fastest there); (4) batched-decode rows — serving decode is
    S_q=batch (8–64), where the plain grid amortizes on its own (the
    split sweep only covers S_q=1; the S_q=64 short shape runs 157
    GB/s unsplit).

## FlyDSL (rocm/flydsl) — probe result: runs on gfx942, D=256 wrong, ours ~2.7x/byte faster

FlyDSL (ROCm's python-kernel DSL, the repo that now carries the
MLA/flash kernels tilelang could not compile) was probed on the same
node as a candidate missing-baseline source. Setup: `pip install
flydsl` (wheel 0.3.2, python3.11) + `torch 2.9.1+rocm6.3` + a repo
checkout for the `kernels/` package; the wheel's MLIR runtime links
`libamdhip64.so.7`, absent on this ROCm 6.3 node, so a compat symlink
(`libamdhip64.so.7 -> /opt/rocm-6.3.0/lib/libamdhip64.so.6`) is needed
(kernels launch and compute through it; a few benign
`hipErrorIllegalState` messages appear at warmup).

`flydsl_flash_attn_func` (gfx942 generic route, dense bf16) at the
GLM-5.3-Flash decode memory pattern (Sq=1, Skv=2048, H=64 — one q row
per head streaming all keys, structurally identical traffic to our
sparse forward at topk=2048 minus the gather):

| shape (dense) | med us | bytes | GB/s | output vs fp32 reference |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---|
| H=64, D=128, Skv=2048 | 208 | 67 MB | 322 | **correct** (maxrel 0.005) |
| H=64, D=256, Skv=2048 | 218 | 134 MB | 615 | **WRONG** (maxrel 27) |
| H=8, D=256, Skv=2048 / H=16, D=256 / H=64, D=256, Skv=512 | ~ | ~ | ~ | **WRONG** (maxrel 11–30) — D=256 breaks regardless of H, Skv |
| H=64, D=576 (DSv3) | — | — | — | launch-time assertion (unsupported) |
| tiny (Sq=128, Skv=128, H=8, D=64) | 213 | — | — | correct; ~200 us DSL-runtime floor on small shapes |

Findings:

  * **Not usable as the DSA baseline.** It is dense-only (no topk-gather
    sparse kernel ships), and its gfx942 generic path is numerically
    broken at `head_dim == 256` — exactly GLM-5.3-Flash's shape — while
    D=128 verifies to bf16 tolerance. (Upstream bug, D=256-conditional,
    independent of H/Skv; worth filing.)
  * **But the perf signal validates the split-key work.** FlyDSL's
    compiler-tuned dense decode moves 67 MB in 208 us (322 GB/s); our
    split sparse kernel moves 134 MB (2x the bytes, D=256 + gather) in
    156 us (~860 GB/s true; the table's 430 GB/s uses the repo byte
    convention that counts the kv term once — see note). Same node, same
    pattern: **~2.7x more bandwidth per byte** than FlyDSL's flash
    codegen at the shapes that matter. Pre-split (3.12 ms), FlyDSL would
    have beaten our kernel by 14x — the gap was exactly the one the
    split path closed.
  * **Byte-model note (this doc).** The `GB/s` column above and in the
    tables counts kv bytes once per head per read-pass (repo-wide
    convention inherited from the original roofline script); FlyDSL's
    probe model counts K and V separately. The 430-vs-860 GB/s
    difference is bookkeeping, not physics — latency comparisons are
    model-free.
  * Remaining use: an authoring stack for future kernels (encodes the
    MFMA fragment layout at a higher level than our hand-written
    `gemm_bf16.hip`, autotunes, and its `mla_fwd_decode` fp8/MFMA
    decode-kernel design targets gfx950 MFMA — a candidate for the
    gfx950 port) — gated on the D=256 bug and the ROCm-7 wheel
    dependency being fixed.

Reproduce:

```bash
# on a beverin mi300 node (gfx942), after pip install flydsl torch (rocm6.3 index)
ln -sf /opt/rocm-6.3.0/lib/libamdhip64.so.6 ~/flydsl-compat/libamdhip64.so.7
git clone --depth 1 https://github.com/rocm/flydsl.git ~/FlyDSL
srun --partition=mi300 -N1 -G1 bash -c 'PATH=$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH \
  PYTHONPATH=$HOME/FlyDSL LD_LIBRARY_PATH=$HOME/flydsl-compat python3.11 flydsl_probe.py'
```

## Caveats and notes

  * **Clocks.** `rocm-smi --setperflevel high` is not permitted on this
    cluster; idle sclk was 95–96 MHz. Variance-driven iteration (median
    over ≥ 20 reps, CV < 3%) keeps the reported medians stable, but
    absolute µs are upper bounds; the roofline ratios and the topk/BQ
    scalings are the robust signals.
  * **Timing methodology.** `hipEventElapsedTime` around single launches;
    sub-µs rows print `<res` (below event resolution). All rows here are
    well above resolution except none — every dsa row is ≥ 200 µs.
  * **Event 0.0 quirk (fixed this run).** With rapid-fire event pairs
    around DVFS clock transitions, ROCm 6.3 occasionally reports an
    elapsed of exactly 0.0 even though the kernels ran (verified by
    output checksum on the affected configs) — this produced `0.0 us /
    inf GB/s` rows in the first split sweep at flaky positions
    (topk=256/split=16, then topk=128/splits 8+16 on the re-run). All
    six bench harnesses now discard non-positive samples
    (`bench_us`/`measure_once`); the stored log is from the fixed
    harness and has no such rows.
  * **Login-node gotcha (probe debugging).** HIP launches on the beverin
    login nodes silently no-op (no gfx942 agent): hipMalloc/memcpy
    succeed, `hipGetLastError` stays clean, outputs stay zeroed, and
    event pairs read ~4 µs. Any standalone probe must run under
    `srun --partition=mi300` — the script does, ad-hoc ssh one-liners
    must too.
  * **Tiny-shape harness fix (this run).** `test_dsa_correct.hip`'s two
    `topk=2` hand-check shapes predated the issue-#59 precondition
    enforcement (`topk % (block_I·inner_iter) == 0`) and aborted the
    whole binary with an uncaught `std::invalid_argument` — on main,
    since #59, the device gate has been unrunnable as written. Fixed by
    giving the tiny cases `block_I = topk` (tiling does not change the
    result); the nine service shapes are untouched.
  * **Same-build indexer numbers** are included in the raw log (section
    5): they match [`../dsa-topk/gfx942.md`](../dsa-topk/gfx942.md)
    within noise (mfma variant fastest, split_kv 4.7× at bs=1).
  * The WIP tree benchmarked here also carries the in-flight `fits_lds`
    cap-parameterization + wmma admission work (GB10 CUDA port); none of
    it touches the gfx942 forward path measured above.

## Reproduce

```bash
# on a beverin mi300 node (gfx942):
rsync -aC --exclude build* --exclude .git ./ beverin:vkernels/
srun --partition=mi300 -N1 -G1 --time=00:40:00 \
  bash meta/scripts/run_dsa_mhc_bench_mi300.sh
# raw log of the run above: beverin-dsa-bench.log
```

## Journal

Benchmarked the issue-#51 DSA sparse-MLA forward on CSCS beverin
(nid002664, MI300A) — the last GLM-5.3-Flash kernel group without perf
numbers. One blocker surfaced immediately: the device correctness gate
aborted on the tiny hand-check shapes because issue #59's precondition
enforcement (`topk % (block_I·inner_iter) == 0`) landed after the test
was written — a pre-existing main breakage, fixed by passing
`block_I = topk` for those two rows (the grouping is
result-independent). With the gate green (11/11), the benchmark exposes
a clear story: prefill runs at 21–28% of the HBM roof, but decode is
occupancy-bound — 64 blocks on 228 CUs streaming `topk` keys serially —
0.4% of the HBM roof and ~0.3% of L2 bandwidth, scaling linearly with
topk (0.20/0.40/3.12 ms at topk=128/256/2048 per layer). The BQ
autotuner confirms tiles are not the issue (< 6% spread). The highest-
leverage follow-on is split_kv for the forward (the indexer already
proved 4.7× from exactly that), then double-buffered key tiles and an
MFMA dot. The full stack now has measured numbers: indexer → kpool →
sparse fwd, plus MHC pre/post (see [`../mhc/gfx942.md`](../mhc/gfx942.md)).

Follow-up run (same node class, nid002424): implemented the split-key
decode — `dsa_sparse_fwd_split` (partial kernel writing normalized fp32
partials + per-split lse over a contiguous topk chunk, then a
log2-domain combine) with the recommendation helper
`dsa_sparse_fwd_split_for` and a split sweep in `bench_dsa.hip`. First
merge attempt was WRONG in an instructive way: weighting the
UNNORMALIZED per-split numerators by 2^(lse_s − m) — the lse came out
exact while outputs were off by 1.1–11x, because the correct weight
applies to the NORMALIZED per-split output (num/row_sum); one-line fix,
now 17/17 vs the oracle including uneven splits. The sweep killed two
assumptions: (1) the CU-filling split formula is 5–6x off at H=64 (best
is 64 at topk=2048, over-subscribing ~18 waves — the binding constraint
is the per-block serial key chain, so `split_for` now recommends
ceil(sqrt(2·topk)), which lands on the measured best on all four
shapes); (2) the bench's event-timing harness can emit exact-0.0 samples
under DVFS transitions — all harnesses now discard them (the flaky
`0.0 us / inf` rows were verified against output checksums before
blaming the kernel). Net: full-topk decode 3.12 → 0.156 ms per layer
(20.0x, 430 GB/s), topk=256 0.40 → 0.059 ms (6.7x), topk=128 0.20 →
0.045 ms (4.5x), DSv3 decode 0.74 → 0.094 ms (7.9x) — the forward no
longer dominates the indexer at any serving shape. Also surveyed
ROCm/FlyDSL for the perf doc's baseline gap and then PROBED it on-node:
it installs on beverin (wheel 0.3.2 + torch 2.9.1+rocm6.3 + a
libamdhip64.so.7 compat shim), its gfx942 dense flash verifies at
D=128 but is numerically WRONG at D=256 (maxrel 27 — the GLM-5.3-Flash
shape, upstream-bug-shaped) and unsupported at D=576, so it cannot
serve as the DSA baseline; at the D=128 decode pattern it moves bytes
at 322 GB/s vs our split kernel's ~860 GB/s true (~2.7x/byte for us).
Recorded in the FlyDSL section above with reproduce steps.

# mhc — Multi-head hybrid-attention pre/post (AMD gfx942, MI300A)

Latency + roofline characterization of the two GLM-5.3-Flash /
DeepSeek-V3 MHC kernels in `src/c/vkernels/kernels/mhc.{cpp,hip}`
(issue #51 part 2) — the pre-attention stage-0 GEMM + squared-sum and the
post-attention combine, whose tilelang forms JIT-abort on gfx942 (dynamic
shared > 64 KB non-optin cap), so there is **no tilelang baseline delta
measurable on this hardware**.

$$\text{pre: } \text{out}[n,o] = \sum_h x[n,h]\,\text{fn}[o,h],\quad \text{sqrsum}[n] = \sum_h x[n,h]^2$$

$$\text{post: } \text{out}[n,j,h] = c[n,j]\,d[n,h] + \textstyle\sum_k a[n,k,j]\,b[n,k,h]$$

**Implementation under test** (see [`docs/kernels/mhc.md`](../../kernels/mhc.md)):
CPU fp32 oracles (always compiled) + HIP kernels using *static* shared
memory sized to fit MI300A's 64 KB non-optin cap (no
`hipFuncSetAttribute` opt-in, no `hidden_block 256 -> 128` patch):

  * `mhc_pre_gemm_sqrsum` — one block per **token** (`grid(num_tokens)`),
    the block's threads split the `hc_mult3` output columns, staging
    `x` once through a static bf16 shared buffer; fp32 accumulation of
    both `out` and `sqrsum`.
  * `mhc_post` — one block per `(token, output head j)`
    (`grid(num_tokens, hc)`), fp32 accumulators, bf16 store.

## Correctness (on the bench node)

Device-vs-oracle **11/11 PASS** (5 pre rows incl. the GLM-5.3
`hc_hidden=16384` and the wider `28672` branch, 6 post rows incl.
`hidden=4096/7168`): pre max_rel ≤ 2.0e-5 (fp32 storage), post max_rel
≤ 3.9e-3 (the documented bf16 round-trip residual).

## Workload

GLM-5.3 MHC shapes: `hc_mult=4, hidden=4096 → hc_hidden=16384,
hc_mult3=24` (decode `n=1` and a 7-token micro-batch) and the wider
`hidden=7168 → hc_hidden=28672` branch. Roof: 1307 TFLOP/s bf16,
5300 GB/s HBM3, ridge ≈ 247 FLOP/B.

## Results — `hip::mhc_pre_gemm_sqrsum` (nid002664, 2026-09-08)

| n | hc_hidden | hc_mult3 | us(min) | us(med) | TFLOP/s | GB/s | AI | bound |
|--:|----------:|---------:|--------:|--------:|--------:|-----:|---:|-------|
| 1 | 4 | 8 | 0.0 | 0.0 | <res | <res | 0.4 | mem |
| 1 | 16384 | 24 | 271.0 | 278.4 | 0.003 | 5.8 | 0.5 | mem |
| 7 | 16384 | 24 | 274.6 | 281.2 | 0.020 | 6.4 | 3.2 | mem |
| 1 | 28672 | 24 | 464.4 | 477.2 | 0.003 | 5.9 | 0.5 | mem |

## Results — `hip::mhc_post`

| n | hc | hidden | us(min) | us(med) | TFLOP/s | GB/s | AI | bound |
|--:|---:|-------:|--------:|--------:|--------:|-----:|---:|-------|
| 1 | 2 | 2 | 0.0 | 0.0 | <res | <res | 0.5 | mem |
| 1 | 4 | 4096 | 0.0 | 0.0 | <res | <res | 2.2 | mem |
| 7 | 4 | 4096 | 0.0 | 0.0 | <res | <res | 2.2 | mem |
| 1 | 4 | 7168 | 0.0 | 0.0 | <res | <res | 2.2 | mem |
| 4 | 8 | 1024 | 0.0 | 0.0 | <res | <res | 4.2 | mem |

Summary (README format):

| Implementation | Time (ms) | Workload | Achieved GFLOPS | Delta to Baseline | Reproduce Script | Note |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| tilelang `mhc_pre_gemm_sqrsum` / `mhc_post` | — | GLM-5.3 MHC shapes | — | — | — | JIT-abort on gfx942 (dynamic shared > 64 KB non-optin cap; the issue-#51 part-2 blocker) |
| vkernels HIP `mhc_pre_gemm_sqrsum` | 0.278 | n=1, hc_mult=4, hidden=4096 (GLM-5.3 decode) | 3 | n/a (baseline faults) | `meta/scripts/run_dsa_mhc_bench_mi300.sh` | single-block at decode |
| vkernels HIP `mhc_pre_gemm_sqrsum` | 0.281 | n=7, hc_mult=4, hidden=4096 | 20 | n/a | same | ~flat vs n=1 |
| vkernels HIP `mhc_pre_gemm_sqrsum` | 0.477 | n=1, hc_mult=4, hidden=7168 | 3 | n/a | same | wider branch |
| vkernels HIP `mhc_post` | < 0.0005 | n=1..7, hc=4, hidden=4096/7168 | — | n/a | same | below event-timer resolution; negligible |

## The pre kernel is single-block-bound at decode; post is noise

  * **`mhc_pre_gemm_sqrsum` launches one block per token** — at decode
    (`n=1`) the entire GEMM runs on **1 of 228 CUs**, streaming the
    1.5 MB `fn` matrix through one block: 5.8 GB/s = 0.1% of the HBM
    roof (the working set is L2-resident; the block is latency-bound on
    the serial `hc_hidden` walk per output column, and the baseline
    re-streams `fn` per column un-coalesced — the tiled, swizzled-shared
    follow-on's target).
  * **n=7 costs the same as n=1** (281 vs 278 µs): the +6 blocks add
    parallelism for free; per-token marginal cost is ~0.4 µs once the
    one-block floor (≈ 270 µs) is amortized.
  * **Serving takeaway**: pre is ~0.28 ms per layer per decode step at
    GLM-5.3-Flash — comparable to the DSA indexer stage and worth a
    split-token/parallel-column redesign, but far below the sparse
    forward's decode cost (see [`../dsa/gfx942.md`](../dsa/gfx942.md)).
  * **`mhc_post` is below the event-timer floor at every serving shape**
    (< ~0.5 µs): with `hc=4, hidden=4096` the kernel moves ~0.5 MB in
    4 blocks — effectively free; no optimization warranted.

## Caveats and notes

  * **Clocks.** `rocm-smi --setperflevel high` is not permitted on this
    cluster; idle sclk was 95–96 MHz. Medians over ≥ 20 reps with CV <
    3% are stable, but absolute µs are upper bounds; ratios and scalings
    are the robust signals.
  * **`<res` rows.** Single-launch `hipEventElapsedTime` cannot resolve
    sub-µs kernels on MI300A (~0.5 µs event floor + dynamic-sclk domain
    changes); the `mhc_post` serving shapes and the n=1 tiny-control row
    print `<res`/0.0. If a precise post number is ever needed, batch
    2000 launches per sample as `bench_dsa_kpool.hip` does.
  * **The 28672-wide pre row runs within the static-smem budget** (56 KB
    < 64 KB non-optin cap) — this is the shape the tilelang path cannot
    even JIT; measured here with no `hidden_block 256 -> 128` patch.
  * Same-build caveat as the DSA doc: the WIP tree carries the in-flight
    GB10 CUDA-port refactor; the gfx942 MHC path is untouched by it.

## Reproduce

```bash
# on a beverin mi300 node (gfx942):
rsync -aC --exclude build* --exclude .git ./ beverin:vkernels/
srun --partition=mi300 -N1 -G1 --time=00:40:00 \
  bash meta/scripts/run_dsa_mhc_bench_mi300.sh
# raw log of the run above: beverin-mhc-bench.log
```

## Journal

Benchmarked the issue-#51 part-2 MHC pre/post kernels on CSCS beverin
(nid002664, MI300A) alongside the DSA forward (one shared run script,
`run_dsa_mhc_bench_mi300.sh`). Correctness was green on the first full
run (11/11) after the DSA-side tiny-shape fix. The numbers say: the
kernels are correct-but-underparallelized rather than kernel-bound —
pre launches one block per token, so decode GEMM work sits on a single
CU at 0.1% of the HBM roof (~278 µs/layer), while post is sub-µs and
effectively free. No tilelang baseline exists on gfx942 (JIT abort), so
the delta column is n/a by construction; the honest comparison is the
sglang-side alternative of patching tilelang's `hidden_block 256->128`,
which these HIP kernels make unnecessary. Future work: split the pre
kernel's output columns across more blocks (or batch tokens per block)
to lift the one-CU floor, and re-measure once the cluster permits
pinning clocks.
