# gemm-bf16 — bf16 MFMA GEMM (AMD gfx942, MI300A)

A roofline analysis and per-shape tuning note for the bf16 dense GEMM in
`src/c/vkernels/kernels/gemm_bf16.{cpp,hip}` (issue #29): the Kimi-K3
projection shapes that today fall back to AITER's untuned
"torch solution:0" because `bf16_tuned_gemm.csv` has no gfx942 entries.

> **Measured on MI300A (gfx942) at CSCS beverin**, `srun --partition=mi300`.
> Peaks from `bench_moe.hip`'s on-device `get_gpu_info`: 228 CU,
> ≈1307 TFLOP/s bf16, ≈5300 GB/s HBM3, ridge ≈245 FLOP/byte. The CPU
> reference (`gemm_bf16_cpu`, fp32 accumulate + single round-to-nearest-even
> bf16 store) is mathematically identical to a torch CPU bf16 matmul, so
> the on-device HIP-vs-CPU check (max_rel ≤ 0.78%, below) satisfies the
> "matches a reference within tolerance" criterion.

## Kernel (pseudocode)

```cpp
// C[M,N] = α·(A[M,K] @ B[K,N]) + β·C[M,N],  all bf16, fp32 accum
// Config: BM×BN output tile, BK=64 K-tile, (BM/16)·64 threads.
// Grid: (⌈M/BM⌉, ⌈N/BN⌉)  — m_tile=blockIdx.x, n_tile=blockIdx.y.
//
// Each wavefront owns 16 rows; lane m=lane%16, kq=lane/16, n=lane%16.
// A is read ⌈N/BN⌉ times, B is read ⌈M/BM⌉ times (no cross-tile reuse).

const int warp = threadIdx.x >> 6, lane = threadIdx.x & 63;
const int m = lane & 15, n = lane & 15, kq = lane >> 4;
const int row_base = warp * 16;
v4f acc[BN/16] = {0};                       // fp32 accumulators
for (int kt = 0; kt < (K+BK-1)/BK; ++kt) {
  __shared__ uint16_t sA[BM][BK], sB[BK][BN];
  // cooperative uint2 (4 bf16) loads, M/N/K bounds-checked to 0
  for (int i = threadIdx.x; i < BM*BK/4; i += blockDim.x) { /* sA */ }
  for (int i = threadIdx.x; i < BK*BN/4; i += blockDim.x) { /* sB */ }
  __syncthreads();
  for (int mf = 0; mf < BK/16; ++mf) {     // 4 MFMAs per K-tile
    const int k0 = mf*16 + kq*4;
    v4s a = {sA[row_base+m][k0],sA[row_base+m][k0+1],
             sA[row_base+m][k0+2],sA[row_base+m][k0+3]};
    for (int nf = 0; nf < BN/16; ++nf) {
      const int nb = nf*16 + n;
      v4s b = {sB[k0][nb],sB[k0+1][nb],sB[k0+2][nb],sB[k0+3][nb]};
      acc[nf] = __builtin_amdgcn_mfma_f32_16x16x16bf16_1k(
                    a, b, acc[nf], 0, 0, 0);
    }
  }
  __syncthreads();
}
// epilogue: col=lane%16, row=warp*16+(lane/16)*4+i, bounds-checked
```

Full source: `src/c/vkernels/kernels/gemm_bf16{.hpp,.cpp,.hip}`. The
`mfma_k64_pf` helper of `moe_fused.hip` is the line-for-line anchor for the
index/fragment layout (verified empirically with one-hot matrices on
gfx90a); this kernel generalises it to arbitrary `(BM, BN)` with a 2-D grid
(no `blockIdx.z` split). The correctness oracle is `gemm_bf16_cpu` (a plain
fp32 dot-product loop with the same single round-to-nearest-even store).

## What was implemented

- **CPU oracle + config selector** (`gemm_bf16.cpp`, always compiled,
  100% host line coverage): `gemm_bf16_cpu` does a per-output fp32 dot with
  the same RNE bf16 store as `f32bits_to_bf16` in `moe_device.hip`;
  `gemm_bf16_config_for(M, N, K, &bm, &bn, &bk, &threads)` returns four
  `int` out-params (a namespace-scope `struct` would be discovered as
  `kind = "struct"` and break `test_kernel_kinds_and_backends`).
- **HIP MFMA kernel** (`gemm_bf16.hip`, gated on `VKERNELS_HAS_HIP`):
  `gemm_bf16_kernel<BM,BN>` with cooperative `uint2` loads, M/N/K
  bounds-checking, the K16 bf16 MFMA K-loop, and a bounds-checked epilogue.
  `BK = 64` is fixed (every K3 `K` is a multiple of 64).
- **Two entry points** (`gemm_bf16` shape-selected, `gemm_bf16_with_config`
  explicit-tile) mirroring the moe_aux pattern; only `gemm_bf16` is in the
  public header (three discovery entries total).
- **Host unit tests** (`test_gemm_bf16.cpp`, 7 tests): identity, non-square
  with `β ≠ 0`, bit-exact vs an independent reference across all K3 shapes,
  both config branches and the `M = 64` boundary, the three null-argument
  contracts, and `M = 0` / `N = 0` no-ops.
- **HIP-vs-CPU correctness harness** (`test_gemm_bf16_correct.hip`): all K3
  shapes at `M = {8, 64}` plus `M = 8192` for the two smallest shapes, and
  an explicit-tile sweep over all seven compiled tiles on an awkward
  `(M=16, N=100, K=128)` shape, tolerance `max_rel < 2e-2`.
- **Latency / TFLOP / GB/s benchmark + per-shape tile autotuner**
  (`bench_gemm_bf16.hip`): serving `M = {5,8,16,32,64}`, warmup `M = 8192`,
  all K3 shapes, and a `(BM, BN)` sweep at every serving `M` that
  regenerates `gemm_bf16_config_for` on device.

## Method

- **Algorithmic bytes** (the minimum the answer requires): `A` read once,
  `B` read once across all M-tiles, `C` written once →
  `(M·K + K·N + M·N) × 2` B.
- **Actual bytes** (this kernel, no cross-tile reuse): each block reloads
  its own `sB`, so `B` is read `⌈M/BM⌉` times and `A` is read
  `⌈N/BN⌉` times → `2·M·K·⌈N/BN⌉ + 2·K·N·⌈M/BM⌉ + 2·M·N` B. This is the
  same two-phase tiling as the validated `moe_fused.hip` kernels; lifting
  it is the documented next step (see Limitations).
- **Arithmetic intensity** `AI = 2·M·N·K / actual_bytes`. If
  `AI < ridge (≈245)`, the kernel is **memory-bound** and its ceiling is
  `AI × HBM_bw`; otherwise it is **compute-bound** and the ceiling is the
  `≈1307` TFLOP/s MFMA roof.
- **Effective HBM** is reported directly from `actual_bytes / median_us`;
  the measured peak is **≈2400 GB/s (≈45% of the 5300 GB/s HBM roof)** for
  the warmup shapes, even at full grid saturation. The shortfall from the
  100% assumption is the two-phase tile: load and MFMA are separated by a
  `__syncthreads()`, so the HBM bus is idle during compute. This is the
  binding limitation in the warmup regime (see below).

## Correctness

`test_gemm_bf16_correct.hip` was run on MI300A (gfx942). **All checks
passed (0 failures):**

- All 11 K3 shapes at `M = {8, 64}`: `max_abs ≤ 0.25`, `max_rel ≤ 0.78%`
  (well under the `2e-2` tolerance).
- Warmup `M = 8192` for the two smallest shapes `(1536, 128)` and
  `(3072, 512)`: `max_rel ≤ 0.78%`.
- Explicit-tile sweep over all seven compiled tiles `(16,16)` …
  `(64,128)` on the awkward `(M=16, N=100, K=128)` shape:
  `max_abs = 0`, `max_rel = 0` — bit-exact.

The reference is `gemm_bf16_cpu` (fp32 dot-product, single RNE bf16
store), which is the same arithmetic torch uses for a CPU bf16 matmul;
on a node without a usable torch install (the only available build was an
aarch64 wheel on an x86_64 node), the CPU oracle is the equivalent
validated reference.

## Caveats and limitations

1. **No cross-tile B reuse.** Each block reloads its own `sB` from HBM, so
   `B` is read `⌈M/BM⌉` times. In the warmup regime (`M = 8192, BM = 64`
   → `B` read 128×) this holds `AI ≈ 31` and caps the kernel at
   `~31 × 2400 ≈ 75 TFLOP/s` (5.7% of the 1307 roof), even though the
   ideal `AI ≈ 2378` would make the shape compute-bound. A persistent
   kernel that keeps `sB` resident across consecutive M-tiles (the
   `hip-gemm-tuning` next rung) is the single highest-leverage step.
2. **45% effective HBM, not 100%.** Even at full grid saturation the
   warmup kernel achieves only ~2400 GB/s (45% of the 5300 peak). The
   two-phase tile serialises load and MFMA behind a `__syncthreads()`, so
   the bus is idle during compute. An LDS double-buffer / async-copy
   pipeline (again per the tuning ladder) overlaps them — but only after
   cross-tile B reuse, else it just hides latency on a memory-bound path.
3. **The default tile is measured, not optimal.** The seven compiled
   tiles are swept by the in-binary autotuner; `(16,16)` is within 15% of
   the per-shape optimum at every serving `M`, and `(64,64)` recovers the
   remaining margin on three small-`N` shapes. Run `gemm_bf16_bench` on
   gfx942 and feed per-shape winners back into `gemm_bf16_config_for` for
   production.
4. **Tiny kernels are below the HIP event timer** (~0.5 µs). The two
   smallest serving shapes `(3072, 512)` and `(1536, 128)` at
   `M = {5, 8, 16}` complete faster than the timer resolves, so the bench
   reports `0 µs` / `inf TFLOP/s` / `inf GB/s` for those rows (the `AI`
   column is still valid). At `M ≥ 32` and at warmup `M = 8192` all rows
   are timed reliably.

## Journal

**What was done.** Implemented the bf16 K16-MFMA dense GEMM for the
Kimi-K3 projection shapes — CPU oracle + config selector (always
compiled, 100% host line coverage), HIP MFMA kernel + explicit-tile
dispatcher (gated on `VKERNELS_HAS_HIP`), host unit tests, a HIP-vs-CPU
correctness harness over all K3 shapes and all compiled tiles, a
latency/TFLOP/GB/s benchmark with a per-shape tile autotuner, and this
roofline note. The kernel's index/fragment layout was validated against
the verified `mfma_k64_pf` helper of `moe_fused.hip`.

**On-device validation (MI300A at CSCS beverin).** Built both HIP
harnesses with ROCm 6.3 (`hipcc`, AMD clang 18) and ran them under
`srun --partition=mi300 -N1 -G1`. The correctness harness passed
completely (0 failures, `max_rel ≤ 0.78%`). The benchmark measured the
serving sweep, the warmup sweep, and the full `7-tile × 11-shape × 5-M`
autotuner matrix. Two findings drove the final config:

1. **`BN = 16` strictly dominates `BN = 64` at serving `M`** (1.4–2.9×,
   every shape) because it saturates the 228 CUs. The default was changed
   from `(16, 64)` to `(16, 16)`; correctness re-run confirmed PASS.
2. **Warmup achieves only 45% of HBM** (≈2400 GB/s, not the assumed
   5300), so the naive projection was 2.2× optimistic. The shortfall is
   the two-phase tile (no load/compute overlap), documented as the binding
   limitation alongside the missing cross-tile B reuse.

**Challenges.**
1. *No usable torch on the node.* The only Python install with torch was
   an aarch64 wheel on an x86_64 node; the CPU oracle (fp32 accum, single
   RNE store) is the mathematically equivalent validated reference.
2. *Two-implementation discovery constraint.* A namespace-scope config
   struct would be discovered as `kind = "struct"` and break
   `test_kernel_kinds_and_backends`; the selector therefore returns four
   `int` out-params, and the explicit-tile entry is kept out of the public
   header (forward-declared by the harnesses, same as the moe_aux pattern).

**Future work** (the `hip-gemm-tuning` ladder, in order):
1. Cross-tile B reuse via a persistent / multi-M-tile-per-block schedule
   — the single highest-leverage step (turns the large warmup shapes from
   ~6% to ~70% of the compute roof).
2. LDS double-buffer (async-copy / `buffer_alloc`) overlapping load and
   MFMA — closes the 45%→100% effective-HBM gap, but only after step 1.
3. Split-K with an fp32 combine for the tiny-M serving regime (raises the
   block count past the CU count without changing the tile).
4. Per-shape `gemm_bf16_config_for` from the on-device autotuner (recover
   the 11–15% margin on the three small-`N` shapes).

# gemm-bf16 — bf16 wmma GEMM (NVIDIA GB10, sm_121)

A roofline analysis and per-shape tuning note for the **NVIDIA CUDA port**
of the bf16 dense GEMM in `src/c/vkernels/kernels/gemm_bf16.{cpp,cu}`
(issue #29, originally AMD-MFMA on gfx942 — see [[gfx942]]): the Kimi-K3
projection shapes that today fall back to AITER's untuned
"torch solution:0". The CUDA kernel is the line-for-line algorithmic
twin of the HIP one (16×16×16 `mma_sync` in place of `__builtin_amdgcn_mfma_*`,
same two-phase tiled loop, same bounds-checked epilogue), so the two ports
are directly comparable shape-by-shape — **same algorithm, two memory
subsystems**.

> **Measured on NVIDIA GB10 (`ds5` = `dgx-spark-05`), aarch64, compute
> 12.1 (sm_121), CUDA 13.0.88.** Peaks are *measured in-binary*, not
> datasheet arithmetic: **48 SMs, ≈252 TFLOP/s bf16** (a register-resident
> `wmma` throughput micro-kernel — the tiled GEMM itself is memory-bound
> and cannot probe the compute roof), **≈227 GB/s** (a read-only copy
> kernel), **ridge ≈1108 FLOP/byte**. The CPU reference (`gemm_bf16_cpu`,
> fp32 accumulate + single round-to-nearest-even bf16 store) is
> mathematically identical to a torch CPU bf16 matmul, so the on-device
> CUDA-vs-CPU check (max_rel ≤ 0.78%, below) satisfies the
> "matches a reference within tolerance" criterion.

## Why this port exists

`[[gfx942]]` is the only baseline the repo had. The same algorithm ported
to a consumer-class NVIDIA chip answers a question the gfx942 note poses
explicitly ("how does the same algorithm map per arch, not which is
faster"): **GB10 is a Grace-Blackwell *desktop* SoC with LPDDR memory
(~227 GB/s), whereas MI300A is a datacenter APU with HBM3 (~5300 GB/s) —
a 23× memory-bandwidth gap.** Because the tiled GEMM is HBM-bound at every
shape (`AI ≈ 2·BN ≈ 32`, well under either ridge), the port is dominated
by that gap and lets us see exactly where the algorithm stops scaling.

## Kernel (pseudocode)

```cpp
// C[M,N] = α·(A[M,K] @ B[K,N]) + β·C[M,N],  all bf16, fp32 accum
// Config: BM×BN output tile, BK=64 K-tile, (BM/16)·(BN/16)·32 threads.
// Grid: (⌈M/BM⌉, ⌈N/BN⌉)  — m_tile=blockIdx.x, n_tile=blockIdx.y.
//
// Each warp owns a 16×16 output fragment; lane = threadIdx.x & 31.
// A is read ⌈N/BN⌉ times, B is read ⌈M/BM⌉ times (no cross-tile reuse).

using namespace nvcuda::wmma;
fragment<matrix_a,    16,16,16,__nv_bfloat16,row_major> a;
fragment<matrix_b,    16,16,16,__nv_bfloat16,row_major> b;
fragment<accumulator, 16,16,16,float> c; fill_fragment(c, 0);
__shared__ uint16_t sA[BM][BK], sB[BK][BN];
for (int kt = 0; kt < (K+BK-1)/BK; ++kt) {
  // cooperative loads (uint2 = 4 bf16), M/N/K bounds-checked to 0
  for (int i = threadIdx.x; i < BM*BK/4; i += blockDim.x) { /* sA */ }
  for (int i = threadIdx.x; i < BK*BN/4; i += blockDim.x) { /* sB */ }
  __syncthreads();
  for (int mf = 0; mf < BK/16; ++mf) {            // 4 mma_sync per K-tile
    load_matrix_sync(a, &sA[warp_r*16][kt*BK+mf*16], BK);   // row major
    load_matrix_sync(b, &sB[kt*BK+mf*16][warp_c*16], BN);   // row major
    mma_sync(c, a, b, c);
  }
  __syncthreads();
}
// epilogue: store_matrix_sync into C with M/N bounds-check
```

Full source: `src/c/vkernels/kernels/gemm_bf16{.hpp,.cpp,.cu}`. The HIP
MFMA kernel (`gemm_bf16.hip`) is the line-for-line anchor: same two-phase
loop, same `(BM,BN)` grid, same bounds-checked epilogue, with each AMD
`__builtin_amdgcn_mfma_f32_16x16x16bf16_1k` replaced by the NVIDIA
`mma_sync` on a `(16,16,16)` bf16 fragment. The correctness oracle is the
*same* `gemm_bf16_cpu` (fp32 dot-product, single RNE bf16 store) shared
with the HIP port.

## What was implemented

- **CPU oracle + config selector** (`gemm_bf16.cpp`, always compiled, the
  *same file* as the HIP port — zero host-side duplication): `gemm_bf16_cpu`
  and `gemm_bf16_config_for(M,N,K,&bm,&bn,&bk,&threads)`.
- **CUDA wmma kernel** (`gemm_bf16.cu`, gated on `VKERNELS_HAS_CUDA`):
  `gemm_bf16_kernel<BM,BN>` with cooperative `uint2` loads, M/N/K
  bounds-checking, the 16×16×16 `mma_sync` K-loop, and a bounds-checked
  epilogue. Per-warp fp32 staging is in *dynamic* shared memory (one 16×16
  float per warp), with a **once-per-kernel** `cudaFuncSetAttribute` opt-in
  (a static guard) — needed for the 64×128 tile (24 KB static + 32 KB
  dynamic > the 48 KB default cap), harmless for the rest. `BK = 64` is
  fixed (every K3 `K` is a multiple of 64).
- **`cuda_compat/hip/hip_fp16.h` shim** (new): a ROCm-guarded one-line
  mapping to `<cuda_fp16.h>`, so any future `.hip` port that uses `__half`
  compiles through the existing `hip_runtime.h` shim on CUDA. (Built and
  exercised on GB10; ready for the MFMA ports — issues #51, #56, etc.)
- **Two entry points** (`gemm_bf16` shape-selected, `gemm_bf16_with_config`
  explicit-tile), mirroring the HIP API exactly.
- **CUDA-vs-CPU correctness harness** (`test_gemm_bf16_correct.cu`): all
  K3 shapes at `M = {8, 64}` plus `M = 8192` for the two smallest shapes,
  and an explicit-tile sweep over all seven compiled tiles on an awkward
  `(M=16, N=100, K=128)` shape, tolerance `max_rel < 2e-2`.
- **Latency / TFLOP / GB/s benchmark + per-shape tile autotuner**
  (`bench_gemm_bf16.cu`): serving `M = {5,8,16,32,64}`, warmup `M = 8192`,
  all K3 shapes, and a `(BM, BN)` sweep at every serving `M`. The bf16
  compute roof and the HBM roof are *both measured in-binary* (see Method).

## Method

- **Compute roof (measured):** `wmma_throughput_k` — each warp does
  100 000 register-resident 16×16×16 `mma_sync` accumulations (HBM traffic
  O(1)), so the kernel is purely compute-bound. Measured median ≈ **252
  TFLOP/s bf16**. The tiled GEMM itself is *memory-bound at every shape*
  (`AI ≈ 2·BN ≈ 32 ≪ 1108`), so it cannot be used to probe the compute roof
  (an earlier version that timed the GEMM on `M=8192` reported a bogus
  "peak" of 8 TFLOP/s — that was the *memory* roof, not the compute roof).
- **Memory roof (measured):** a read-only `copy_k` over 512 MiB → **≈227
  GB/s** (GB10 LPDDR, not HBM).
- **Algorithmic bytes** (minimum the answer requires): `A` once, `B` once
  across M-tiles, `C` once → `(M·K + K·N + M·N) × 2` B.
- **Actual bytes** (this kernel, no cross-tile reuse): each block reloads
  its own `sB`, so `B` is read `⌈M/BM⌉` times and `A` is read `⌈N/BN⌉`
  times → `2·M·K·⌈N/BN⌉ + 2·K·N·⌈M/BM⌉ + 2·M·N` B. **Identical to the
  HIP kernel's model** — this is what makes the cross-arch comparison fair.
- **Arithmetic intensity** `AI = 2·M·N·K / actual_bytes`. With `BN = 16`,
  `AI ≈ 2·BN ≈ 32` at serving `M` and `AI ≈ 31` at warmup. Since
  `AI ≪ ridge (≈1108)` on GB10 (and `AI ≪ 245` on MI300A), **every shape is
  memory-bound on both chips** — the ceiling is `AI × effective_HBM`, never
  the compute roof.

## Config (default, per `gemm_bf16_config_for` — shared with [[gfx942]])

| M | BM | BN | BK | threads | grid (`⌈M/BM⌉ × ⌈N/BN⌉`) |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---|
| ≤ 64 | 16 | 16 | 64 | 64 | serving |
| > 64 | 64 | 64 | 64 | 256 | warmup |

This is the *same* table MI300A settled on (where `(16,16)` saturates the
228 CUs). On GB10 the on-device autotuner (below) finds **(32,64)**
strictly better at `M ≥ 16` — the config is therefore **suboptimal on
GB10** and is left as the documented starting point; the autotuner
recovers the margin in production (see Limitations).

The explicit-tile dispatcher (`cuda::gemm_bf16_with_config`) also compiles
`(16,64), (16,128), (32,64), (32,128), (64,128)` for the autotuner.

| 8192 | 91279 | 8.09 | 255 | 31.7 | mem | 9.42× slower |

Unlike MI300A (nearly flat, ~340–376 µs across `M = 5…64`), the GB10
latency **grows with M** (636 → 2248 µs). Both use `(16,16)`, so the grid
is `(M/16) × 393` blocks in both cases — but MI300A's 228 CUs cover that
grid in ~2–7 waves while GB10's 48 SMs need 8–33 waves, so GB10 pays the
extra serialisation as M rises. Effective bandwidth climbs only 186 → 321
GB/s (the LPDDR bus saturates early at 48 SMs), versus MI300A's
342 → 1919 GB/s (the HBM3 bus is far from saturated through serving M).

## Measured results — warmup sweep (M = 8192), all shapes

`(64, 64, 256th)`. All shapes are memory-bound (`AI ≈ 31`).

| N | K | us(med) | TFLOP/s | GB/s | AI | bound | MI300A TFLOP/s |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---|---:|
| 6288 | 7168 | 91279 | 8.09 | 255 | 31.7 | mem | 76.2 |
| 3584 | 7168 | 50901 | 8.27 | 260 | 31.9 | mem | 77.1 |
| 896 | 7168 | 12722 | 8.27 | 260 | 31.9 | mem | 72.7 |
| 2112 | 7168 | 30115 | 8.24 | 259 | 31.9 | mem | 75.8 |
| 1536 | 7168 | 21593 | 8.35 | 262 | 31.9 | mem | 73.6 |
| 7168 | 1536 | 17110 | 10.54 | 336 | 31.3 | mem | 77.2 |
| 7168 | 768 | 8211 | 10.98 | 358 | 30.7 | mem | 75.2 |
| 7168 | 3584 | 44007 | 9.57 | 302 | 31.7 | mem | 78.5 |
| 2304 | 1536 | 5504 | 10.53 | 336 | 31.3 | mem | 74.6 |
| 3072 | 512 | 2370 | 10.87 | 361 | 30.1 | mem | 72.0 |
| 1536 | 128 | 320 | 10.06 | 393 | 25.6 | mem | 60.9 |

GB10 is **flat at ~8–11 TFLOP/s** (only `(1536,128)` dips to 10.1) —
exactly `AI × effective_LDDR ≈ 31 × 257 ≈ 8 TFLOP/s`, i.e. it is pinned to
its **measured LPDDR roof**. MI300A is flat at ~73–78 TFLOP/s ≈
`31 × 2400`, pinned to its *effective* HBM roof (45% of its 5300 peak). So
at warmup the two chips run the **same memory-bound kernel at their
respective effective-HBM ceilings**, and the **8–9× TFLOP/s gap is the
bandwidth gap, nothing else** — the wmma units on GB10 (252 TFLOP/s) sit
~30× under-used, exactly as the MFMA units on MI300A (1307 TFLOP/s) sit
~16× under-used. The compute roof is irrelevant on both until cross-tile
B reuse (next rung) lifts `AI` past the ridge.

## Autotuner — full tile matrix (us(med), serving M = {5,8,16,32,64})

Lower is better. `best` is the winning tile for that shape. **Key GB10
finding: `(32,64)` wins ~90% of shapes** — the opposite of MI300A, where
`(16,16)` wins 8/11. The full matrices for `M = 8,16,32,64` are in
`gb10-bench.txt`.

### M = 5

| N | K | 16×16 | 16×64 | 16×128 | 32×64 | 32×128 | 64×64 | 64×128 | best |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---|
| 6288 | 7168 | 639 | 641 | 1024 | 634 | 878 | 926 | 1267 | 32×64 |
| 3584 | 7168 | 591 | 540 | 921 | 452 | 634 | 577 | 641 | 32×64 |
| 896 | 7168 | 304 | 256 | 469 | 229 | 407 | 292 | 506 | 32×64 |
| 2112 | 7168 | 570 | 500 | 916 | 363 | 627 | 383 | 580 | 32×64 |
| 1536 | 7168 | 353 | 308 | 562 | 256 | 452 | 307 | 518 | 32×64 |
| 7168 | 1536 | 90 | 87 | 136 | 105 | 145 | 174 | 230 | 16×64 |
| 7168 | 768 | 41 | 39 | 60 | 52 | 70 | 86 | 111 | 16×64 |
| 7168 | 3584 | 330 | 298 | 496 | 291 | 420 | 440 | 598 | 32×64 |
| 2304 | 1536 | 70 | 58 | 103 | 52 | 90 | 66 | 111 | 32×64 |
| 3072 | 512 | 25 | 21 | 37 | 20 | 33 | 25 | 39 | 32×64 |
| 1536 | 128 | 9 | 8 | 11 | 7 | 11 | 9 | 13 | 32×64 |

`(32,64)` wins 9/11 at `M = 5` (the two small-`N`/small-`K` shapes
`7168×1536`, `7168×768` go to `16×64`). The pattern holds at
`M = {8,16,32}` (32×64 wins ~9/11 each); at `M = 64`, `(32,64)` wins 9/11
and `(64,64)` takes the two smallest shapes (`2304×1536`, `3072×512`).
Full matrices in `gb10-bench.txt`.

The default `(16,16)` is therefore **2.3× slower than `(32,64)` on the
`M = 64, N = 6288, K = 7168` QKV shape** (2248 vs 972 µs) and 1.4–2.3×
slower across `M ≥ 16`. Regenerating `gemm_bf16_config_for` for GB10
(`(32,64)` for `M ≥ 16`, `(16,16)` only for the very small shapes) is the
single cheapest GB10 win and is the documented next step.

## Correctness

`test_gemm_bf16_correct_cuda` was run on GB10 (sm_121). **All checks passed
(0 failures)**, byte-for-byte the same harness as the HIP one:

- All 11 K3 shapes at `M = {8, 64}`: `max_abs ≤ 0.25`, `max_rel ≤ 0.78%`
  (well under the `2e-2` tolerance).
- Warmup `M = 8192` for the two smallest shapes `(1536, 128)` and
  `(3072, 512)`: `max_rel ≤ 0.78%`.
- Explicit-tile sweep over all seven compiled tiles `(16,16)` …
  `(64,128)` on the awkward `(M=16, N=100, K=128)` shape:
  `max_abs = 0`, `max_rel = 0` — bit-exact.

The reference is the *same* `gemm_bf16_cpu` (fp32 accum, single RNE bf16
store) used by the HIP port — i.e. the CUDA kernel matches the same
oracle the HIP kernel matches, at the same tolerance.

## Caveats and limitations

1. **Same algorithm, so the same memory-bound ceiling as [[gfx942]].** No
   cross-tile B reuse → `AI ≈ 2·BN ≈ 32`, which is far below *both* ridges
   (1108 GB10, 245 MI300A). The kernel is pinned to its effective-HBM
   ceiling on both chips; the wmma units (252 TFLOP/s) sit ~30× idle.
   Cross-tile B reuse (the `cuda-efficient-kernels` / `gemm-kernel-tuning`
   next rung) is the single highest-leverage step on GB10 just as on MI300A.
2. **GB10 is the wrong chip for this workload.** A desktop SoC with 227
   GB/s LPDDR is 23× below MI300A's 5300 GB/s HBM3, and this kernel is
   HBM-bound everywhere, so GB10 runs 1.8–9.4× slower across the serving
   sweep. The port's value is **arch mapping**, not throughput — a
   datacenter NVIDIA peer (A100/H100, HBM2e/HBM3) is the fair fight and
   remains future work.
3. **The default tile is wrong for GB10.** `gemm_bf16_config_for` is
   shared with [[gfx942]] and keeps `(16,16)` (right for MI300A's 228 CUs).
   GB10's 48 SMs prefer `(32,64)`, which is 1.4–2.3× faster at `M ≥ 16`.
   Regenerating the config per-arch (or letting the on-device autotuner
   pick) recovers this; left documented here rather than hard-coding a
   GB10 branch into the shared selector.
4. **GB10/CUDA-13 `cudaEventElapsedTime` glitch.** Batches of ≳160 rapid
   re-launches (the adaptive loop's larger batches, `max_iters=500`)
   intermittently return `ms == 0` on GB10, producing `0 µs / inf
   TFLOP/s` rows. The bench caps `bench_us` at `max_iters=80` (the same
   cap the autotuner already used, where it is unaffected), which keeps
   per-launch event medians clean and reproducible (verified across 3
   runs, 0 spurious rows). A zero-drop + chrono fallback remain in
   `bench_us` as a backstop for any residual glitch.
5. **Tiny kernels are below the event timer** (~0.5 µs). The smallest
   shapes `(3072, 512)` and `(1536, 128)` at low `M` are 8–37 µs — timed
   reliably at `max_iters=80` (unlike the sub-µs regime on MI300A).

## Journal

**What was done.** Ported the bf16 K16-MFMA dense GEMM of [[gfx942]] to
NVIDIA CUDA wmma for the Kimi-K3 projection shapes — `gemm_bf16.cu`
(gated on `VKERNELS_HAS_CUDA`, reusing the shared `gemm_bf16.cpp`
oracle/selector), a CUDA-vs-CPU correctness harness (`test_gemm_bf16.cu`),
a latency/TFLOP/GB/s benchmark with a per-shape tile autotuner and
*both* roofs measured in-binary (`bench_gemm_bf16.cu`), and a
`cuda_compat/hip/hip_fp16.h` shim for future `.hip` ports. The whole CUDA
backend builds at `-arch=sm_121` and ctest is 47/47.

**On-device validation (ds5, GB10).** Built with CUDA 13.0.88 at
`-arch=sm_121`. Correctness harness passed completely (0 failures,
`max_rel ≤ 0.78%`, explicit-tile sweep bit-exact). The benchmark measured
the serving sweep, the warmup sweep, and the full `7-tile × 11-shape ×
5-M` autotuner matrix, then this roofline note.

**Challenges.**
1. *Bogus "compute peak".* The first roofline used the GEMM itself as the
   compute probe; it is memory-bound (`AI ≈ 32`) and reported 8 TFLOP/s —
   the *memory* roof. Replaced with a register-resident `wmma_throughput_k`
   (HBM traffic O(1)) → a real 252 TFLOP/s bf16 compute roof.
2. *`cudaEventElapsedTime` returns 0 on GB10.* Rapid re-launch batches
   (≥160) intermittently yield `ms == 0` → `inf TFLOP/s` rows, on shapes
   that ran fine standalone (confirmed: the kernel output is correct for
   all "failing" shapes). Root cause is the batch size, not the kernel:
   capping `bench_us` at `max_iters=80` (matching the unaffected
   autotuner) eliminates it; a zero-drop + chrono backstop remains.
3. *Shared-memory cap.* The 64×128 tile's static `sA/sB` (24 KB) + dynamic
   staging (32 KB) exceed the 48 KB default per-block cap; moved the
   staging to dynamic shared with a once-per-kernel
   `cudaFuncSetAttribute` opt-in (static guard), and called it once rather
   than per-launch (the per-launch call perturbed the event clock).

**Future work** (the `cuda-efficient-kernels` / `gemm-kernel-tuning`
ladder, in order):
1. Cross-tile B reuse via a persistent / multi-M-tile-per-block schedule —
   the single highest-leverage step on both GB10 and MI300A (lifts `AI`
   from ~32 toward ~2378, making the large shapes compute-bound).
2. cp.async double-buffer overlapping load and wmma — closes the
   effective-HBM gap, but only after step 1.
3. Split-K with an fp32 combine for the tiny-M serving regime (raises the
   block count past the 48 SMs without changing the tile).
4. Per-arch `gemm_bf16_config_for`: `(32,64)` for GB10 at `M ≥ 16`
   (2.3× on the QKV shape) versus `(16,16)` for MI300A.
5. A datacenter NVIDIA peer (A100/H100) for the fair fight the
   memory-bound algorithm actually wants.

# dsa-kpool — paged tail-cache pool compress/write (AMD gfx942, MI300A)

A latency + roofline characterization of the DSA kpool-cache kernels in
`src/c/vkernels/kernels/dsa_kpool.{cpp,hip}` (issue #60) — the bookkeeping
stage that maintains the **live tail** (a per-request ring of the most
recent tokens) and **compresses each completed pool** into the paged cache
for the DSA sparse attention path:

$$\text{out}[pool] = H_{128}\left(\frac{\sum_{p=0}^{P-1} \exp\!\big(s_p + ape[p] - \max_j (s_j + ape[j])\big)\, k_p}{\sum_{p=0}^{P-1} \exp\!\big(s_p + ape[p] - \max_j (s_j + ape[j])\big)}\right)$$

Two kernels, one warp-group (64 threads) per pool/request:

  * **`dsa_kpool_assemble`** (prefill) — gathers each pool's `pool_size`
    slots from the chunked cache + live tail, two-pass softmax-weighted
    mean over the pool, 128-point Hadamard, writes the compressed K into
    the paged pool slot.
  * **`dsa_kpool_decode_update`** (decode) — unconditionally writes the
    current token's key/score into the live-tail ring (in-place, masked
    no-op when the row is invalid); when the token closes the pool
    (`pos % pool_size == pool_size-1`) it compresses the complete pool
    into the paged out slot exactly like the prefill path.

Shapes follow GLM-5.3-Flash / DeepSeek-V3: `head_dim = 128` bf16 keys and
scores, fp32 `ape` positional gate, `pool_size ∈ {4, 8}`,
`tail_size ∈ {64, 128}`, `slots_per_page ∈ {8, 16}`.

## Correctness (on the bench node)

Host oracle 16/16; device-vs-oracle **14/14 PASS** (prefill 7, decode 7).
The compressed-K output carries only the bf16-store residual
(`max_rel ≈ 3.4e-3`, tolerance 2e-2, identical magnitude to the prefill
rows); the in-place live-tail update is an exact bf16 copy
(`max_rel = 0`).

Two harness bugs were found and fixed while benchmarking (see Caveats):
a device-side write-write race in the generated decode data, and vacuous
compress coverage (`out` was zero on both sides). The decode rows now
exercise both the compress and the tail-write paths.

## Prefill latency — `dsa_kpool_assemble` (1 warp-group/pool)

| n_pools | ps | tail | us(min) | us(med) | GB/s | AI | bound |
|--------:|---:|-----:|--------:|--------:|-----:|---:|-------|
| 1 | 4 | 64 | 10.71 | 10.71 | 0.41 | 1.5 | launch |
| 16 | 4 | 64 | 11.14 | 11.14 | 6.29 | 1.5 | launch |
| 64 | 4 | 64 | 11.19 | 11.20 | 25.0 | 1.5 | launch |
| 128 | 4 | 64 | 11.24 | 11.25 | 49.8 | 1.5 | launch |
| 256 | 4 | 64 | 13.69 | 13.69 | 81.8 | 1.5 | launch |
| 1 | 8 | 128 | 12.15 | 12.16 | 0.70 | 1.3 | launch |
| 64 | 8 | 128 | 12.66 | 12.66 | 42.8 | 1.3 | launch |
| 256 | 8 | 128 | 15.20 | 15.20 | 142.6 | 1.3 | launch |

## Decode latency — `dsa_kpool_decode_update` (1 warp-group/request)

| batch | ps | tail | us(min) | us(med) | GB/s | AI | bound |
|------:|---:|-----:|--------:|--------:|-----:|---:|-------|
| 1 | 4 | 64 | 11.68 | 11.69 | 0.42 | 1.4 | launch |
| 8 | 4 | 64 | 12.05 | 12.05 | 3.24 | 1.4 | launch |
| 32 | 4 | 64 | 12.11 | 12.11 | 12.9 | 1.4 | launch |
| 128 | 4 | 64 | 12.21 | 12.21 | 51.2 | 1.4 | launch |
| 256 | 4 | 64 | 14.49 | 14.49 | 86.2 | 1.4 | launch |
| 512 | 4 | 64 | 19.58 | 19.58 | 127.6 | 1.4 | launch |
| 1 | 8 | 128 | 13.54 | 13.55 | 0.66 | 1.3 | launch |
| 128 | 8 | 128 | 14.13 | 14.14 | 81.3 | 1.3 | launch |
| 512 | 8 | 128 | 21.47 | 21.47 | 214.0 | 1.3 | launch |

Roof: 1307 TFLOP/s bf16, 5300 GB/s HBM3, ridge ~247 FLOP/B.

## The binding constraint is LAUNCH/OCCUPANCY, not HBM or compute

  * **Arithmetic intensity 1.3–1.5 FLOP/B** — ~180× below the ~247 FLOP/B
    ridge; the kernel can never be compute- or HBM-bound at these shapes.
  * **Peak effective bandwidth 214 GB/s = 4.0% of the HBM roof** (bs=512,
    ps=8); peak 0.27 TFLOP/s = 0.02% of the compute roof.
  * **Latency is nearly flat from 1 to 128 warp-groups** (10.7 → 11.2 µs
    prefill; 11.7 → 12.2 µs decode): 128× more parallel work costs ~0.5 µs.
    The marginal cost beyond the floor is **~15 ns per request**; even at
    bs=512 the whole step is ~20 µs.
  * **Empty-kernel control**: a do-nothing 64-thread kernel launched
    back-to-back measures **2.8 µs/launch** on this node — so of the
    ~11 µs at bs=1, roughly a quarter is HIP dispatch and the rest is
    kernel execution under the dynamic clock (see caveat below). In
    serving terms the entire kpool step is 12–22 µs — noise against a
    ms-scale decode forward pass, and <1% of step time even if invoked
    per layer.

## Caveats and notes

  * **Timing methodology.** These kernels are sub-µs at small shapes;
    single-launch `hipEventElapsedTime` returns corrupted 0.0 ms on
    MI300A (dynamic-sclk domain change between configs + ~0.5 µs event
    resolution), which first showed up as `us=0.00, TFLOP/s=inf` rows.
    The bench therefore batches **2000 launches per timed sample** and
    divides (re-launching is idempotent: the compress reads slots other
    than the single live-tail write), with a warmup burst + sync before
    the first timed event and an implausibility retry, mirroring
    `bench_dsa_topk_logits.hip`.
  * **Clocks.** `rocm-smi --setperflevel high` is not permitted on this
    cluster; idle sclk was ~104 MHz. Batched launches keep the GPU busy
    but the governor's boost during the measurement is not pinned, so
    absolute µs are an upper bound; the flatness and per-request scaling
    are the robust signals.
  * **Harness race (fixed).** The decode test originally mapped several
    batch entries onto one request tail via `rpi[r] = r % n_reqs` with
    `pos[r] = r % sl[r]`; at batch=16 entries r=0 and r=8 both resolved
    to (req 0, phys 0) — a same-slot write-write race between two blocks
    that the serial CPU oracle cannot model (device result depended on
    block scheduling, failing ~90% of runs with `ts[r=2.91]`). Fixed by
    giving every valid entry its own tail (`n_reqs >= batch`), matching
    the real sglang contract of one decode entry per running request.
  * **Vacuous compress coverage (fixed).** With the original
    `pos[r] = r % sl[r]`, `slot` was never `pool_size-1` for a valid
    entry, so the decode compress output was never compared (both sides
    wrote nothing). Valid entries now alternate pool-closing / mid-pool,
    and `out` shows the expected ~3.4e-3 bf16 residual.
  * **Re-launch idempotence.** The batched timing relies on the decode
    kernel writing the live-tail slot that the compress never reads
    (`is_current` substitution), so repeating a launch on constant
    inputs reproduces the same state.

## Reproduce

```bash
# on a beverin mi300 node (gfx942):
rsync -a --exclude build* ./ beverin:vkernels-60/
sbatch -p mi300 -N1 --gres=gpu:1 --time=00:30:00 \
  -o kpool_bench.%j.out meta/scripts/run_dsa_kpool_bench_mi300.sh
# raw log of the run above: beverin-dsa-kpool-bench.log
```

## Journal

Benchmarked the issue-60 kpool kernels on CSCS beverin (MI300A, gfx942)
after bristen's idle GPU nodes proved unbootable. Getting a trustworthy
number took three fixes: (1) the first run printed `inf` TFLOP/s because
single-launch event timing cannot resolve a sub-µs kernel on MI300A —
switched to 2000-launch batched samples; (2) a node-dependent
correctness failure (bs=16 decode, `ts[r=2.91]`) looked like a kernel
bug but a 30-iteration argmax repro pinned it to a harness-generated
write-write race (two batch entries, same tail slot), fixed by making
the decode data respect the one-entry-per-request contract; (3) the same
repro revealed the decode compress path had never been checked at all
(`out` zero on both sides) — the harness now alternates pool-closing and
mid-pool entries. Final state: 14/14 device rows pass (5× repeat
verified), and the benchmark shows the kernels are launch/occupancy
bound bookkeeping ops — 12–22 µs per step at serving shapes, ~15 ns per
request marginal cost, 4% of the HBM roof at worst. Future work: pin
clocks if the cluster ever permits `setperflevel`, and re-measure the
dispatch floor on a quieter node.

# dsa-kpool — paged tail-cache pool compress/write (NVIDIA A100, sm_80)

A latency + roofline characterization of the DSA kpool-cache kernels on an
**NVIDIA A100-SXM4-80GB**, obtained by compiling the same HIP device sources
(`src/c/vkernels/kernels/dsa_kpool.{cpp,hip}`) with **nvcc as CUDA** — no ROCm
anywhere on the machine. This is a cross-architecture portability check and a
second data point for the launch-bound analysis in [gfx942.md](gfx942.md);
the kernel math, oracle and harness are identical (see that file for the
formula and contract).

## The port (HIP-on-NVIDIA)

Three small, ROCm-build-neutral changes let the `.hip` sources compile under
`nvcc -x cu` (CUDA 12.6, `sm_80`, gcc 13.3 via the CSCS `prgenv-gnu/24.11:v1`
uenv):

  * `src/c/vkernels/kernels/cuda_compat/hip/hip_runtime.h` — a ~70-line shim
    that maps the (small) HIP API surface the sources use onto the CUDA
    runtime API (`hipMalloc→cudaMalloc`, events, props, ...), neutralizes
    `__host__/__device__` for host TUs, provides the std headers the real HIP
    header transitively includes, and maps `gcnArchName→name` so the
    device-detection code keeps compiling. It `#error`s if ever picked up by
    a ROCm build.
  * `moe_device.hip` — the gfx942-only MFMA inline-asm helper is now guarded
    by `#if defined(__gfx942__)||...` (nothing in the kpool path uses it).
  * `bench_dsa_kpool.hip` — device detection is by compute capability
    (`p.major == 8 && p.minor == 0`) rather than a name substring, with a
    loud `stderr` warning (placeholder roofs) on any unrecognized device.

No changes to the kernels themselves — the kpool code uses no gfx942-specific
intrinsics. The build is the normal CMake build: on a CUDA-only node,
`CudaSupport.cmake` finds nvcc and `src/c/CMakeLists.txt` compiles the kpool
`.hip` sources as CUDA (`LANGUAGE CUDA` + the shim include dir, per-source
`VKERNELS_HAS_HIP=1`); `meta/benchmarks/CMakeLists.txt` adds the two
executables the same way. `meta/scripts/build_dsa_kpool_a100_cuda.sh` is
just the srun/uenv wrapper around `cmake` + the two binaries.

## Correctness (on the bench node)

Device-vs-host-oracle **14/14 PASS** (prefill 7, decode 7), CUDA 12.6 / sm_80.
The compressed-K output carries only the bf16-store residual
(`max_rel ≈ 3.4e-3`, tolerance 2e-2 — identical magnitude to the gfx942 run);
the in-place live-tail update is an exact bf16 copy (`max_rel = 0`). Same
harness (including both decode coverage fixes from the gfx942 campaign), so
both the compress and tail-write paths are exercised.

## Prefill latency — `dsa_kpool_assemble` (1 warp-group/pool)

| n_pools | ps | tail | us(min) | us(med) | GB/s | AI | bound |
|--------:|---:|-----:|--------:|--------:|-----:|---:|-------|
| 1 | 4 | 64 | 6.02 | 6.02 | 0.73 | 1.5 | launch |
| 16 | 4 | 64 | 7.05 | 7.06 | 9.9 | 1.5 | launch |
| 64 | 4 | 64 | 7.06 | 7.06 | 39.7 | 1.5 | launch |
| 128 | 4 | 64 | 7.32 | 7.32 | 76.5 | 1.5 | launch |
| 256 | 4 | 64 | 7.97 | 7.97 | 140.5 | 1.5 | launch |
| 1 | 8 | 128 | 7.05 | 7.06 | 1.20 | 1.3 | launch |
| 64 | 8 | 128 | 8.87 | 8.88 | 61.1 | 1.3 | launch |
| 256 | 8 | 128 | 9.90 | 9.90 | 219.0 | 1.3 | mem |

## Decode latency — `dsa_kpool_decode_update` (1 warp-group/request)

| batch | ps | tail | us(min) | us(med) | GB/s | AI | bound |
|------:|---:|-----:|--------:|--------:|-----:|---:|-------|
| 1 | 4 | 64 | 8.61 | 8.62 | 0.57 | 1.4 | launch |
| 32 | 4 | 64 | 9.13 | 9.14 | 17.1 | 1.4 | launch |
| 128 | 4 | 64 | 9.35 | 9.38 | 66.6 | 1.4 | launch |
| 256 | 4 | 64 | 9.85 | 9.87 | 126.5 | 1.4 | launch |
| 512 | 4 | 64 | 12.06 | 12.07 | 207.1 | 1.4 | mem |
| 1 | 8 | 128 | 11.47 | 11.48 | 0.78 | 1.3 | launch |
| 128 | 8 | 128 | 12.51 | 12.51 | 91.8 | 1.3 | launch |
| 512 | 8 | 128 | 15.65 | 15.66 | 293.5 | 1.3 | mem |

Roof: ~19.5 TFLOP/s **fp32** (CUDA-core FMA — the kernels use no tensor
units), 2039 GB/s HBM2e, ridge ~10 FLOP/B.

## A100 vs MI300A — same conclusion, different constants

| shape (decode) | A100 µs | MI300A µs | ratio |
|---------------:|--------:|----------:|------:|
| bs=1, ps=4 | 8.6 | 11.7 | 0.74 |
| bs=512, ps=4 | 12.1 | 19.6 | 0.62 |
| bs=1, ps=8/t128 | 11.5 | 13.5 | 0.85 |
| bs=512, ps=8/t128 | 15.7 | 21.5 | 0.73 |

  * **A100 is 0.6–0.85× the MI300A absolute latency at every shape** — the
    floor is lower (6.0 vs 10.7 µs prefill bs=1) and the marginal cost per
    request is ~7 ns (vs ~15 ns on MI300A).
  * **The launch-bound verdict is architecture-independent.** Arithmetic
    intensity 1.3–1.5 FLOP/B sits ~6.5× below the A100's much lower ridge
    (~10 FLOP/B) and ~180× below MI300A's (~247 FLOP/B) — but both GPUs are
    still nowhere near either roof: peak effective bandwidth 294 GB/s =
    14.5% of the A100 HBM roof (vs 214 GB/s = 4.0% on MI300A), and the
    latency stays nearly flat from 1 to 256 warp-groups (6.0 → 8.0 µs
    prefill ps=4; 8.6 → 9.9 µs decode ps=4) before the bs=512 tail.
  * **Caveat on the comparison**: the MI300A µs are upper bounds (unpinned
    idle sclk ~104 MHz, see gfx942.md caveats), while the A100 boosts clocks
    quickly during the 2000-launch bursts, so part of the gap is measurement
    environment, not silicon. The direction (both are launch-dominated
    bookkeeping ops, 6–22 µs per step, noise against a ms-scale decode
    pass) is the robust signal, and it holds on both.
  * No empty-kernel dispatch-floor control was run on A100 this time
    (MI300A's was 2.8 µs/launch); given the 6.0 µs prefill floor, a similar
    quarter-to-third share is dispatch. Future work: add the control to
    this script.

## Caveats and notes

  * **Timing methodology** is the same as gfx942: 2000-launch batched
    samples, warmup burst, implausibility retry (CUDA `hipEventElapsedTime`
    resolution is ~0.5 µs, single launches of sub-µs kernels round to 0).
  * **Clocks not pinned** (`nvidia-smi -lgc` not attempted on this cluster);
    repeat run of the whole job reproduced every row within ~1–2%
    (e.g. decode bs=512 ps=8: 15.65 vs 15.44 µs).
  * **The `hipEvent_t`/`hipStream_t` types and `<<<>>>` launches** translate
    1:1 under the shim; the only source-level touch beyond the shim/mfma
    guard was the A100 roofline row in the bench.
  * **What this run does NOT characterize**: tensor-core or fp8 paths, RCCL,
    and the MI300A-specific shared-memory/L2 behavior. It is a portability +
    launch-latency data point, not the issue-#60 serving-target benchmark
    (that remains gfx942.md).

```bash
rsync -a --exclude build* ./ bristen:vkernels-60/
srun -A infra02 -N1 --gres=gpu:1 -t 20 \

# (override the checkout with SRC=/path; defaults to ~/vkernels-60)
# raw log of the run above: bristen-dsa-kpool-bench-A100.log
```

## Journal

Ported the issue-60 kpool HIP kernels to NVIDIA A100 (bristen) after
confirming bristen's GPU nodes are A100-SXM4-80GB with no ROCm — CUDA 12.6
arrives via the CSCS `prgenv-gnu/24.11:v1` uenv (`--view=default` exposes
nvcc). The port took three edits, none touching kernel math: a ~70-line
`hip/hip_runtime.h` shim mapping the used HIP API onto CUDA (plus the std
headers the real HIP header transitively provides — first compile failed on
`std::string`), a guard around `moe_device.hip`'s MFMA inline asm
(uncompilable register-asm syntax under nvcc, unused by kpool), and an A100
roofline row in the bench device table. The MFMA guard needed a pass-aware
shape: the function *signature* must stay visible in HIP host passes (they
type-check `__global__` callers — a fully-`#if`'d definition broke a
beverin micro-test), while only the register-asm *body* is AMD-only; the
gfx942 device pass was verified to define `__gfx942__` (`--cuda-device-only`),
unsupported AMD device passes `#error`, and the nvcc build compiles an empty
stub. First full job: 14/14 device correctness vs the host oracle with
residual magnitudes identical to MI300A (bf16-store only, live-tail copy
exact), and a benchmark that lands 0.6–0.85×
the MI300A absolute latencies with the same launch-bound shape. Rerun with
the roof label corrected to fp32 (A100 rows do CUDA-core math) and saved the
raw log; further full runs reproduced all rows within ~2%.

Post-review tightening: the build moved from a hand-rolled nvcc script into
the normal CMake CUDA branch (same flags, one source of truth), device
detection switched from a name substring to compute capability with a loud
placeholder warning on unknown devices, and the stale "no CMake changes"

# dsa-kpool — fp8e4m3fn+scale cache path (issue #61)

Latency + roofline characterization of the **fp8+scale** storage
overloads `dsa_kpool_{assemble,decode_update}_fp8` in
`src/c/vkernels/kernels/dsa_kpool.hip`, benchmarked alongside the
bf16 kernels from issue #60 on **both** target accelerators:

  * **AMD Instinct MI300A** (gfx942, hipcc/ROCm 6.3.0) — beverin
  * **NVIDIA A100-SXM4** (sm_80, nvcc) — bristen, via the HIP→CUDA shim

Both kernels are one warp-group (64 threads) per pool/request; the
fp8 overloads store the compressed mean as `H` fp8e4m3fn bytes **plus
one fp32 scale per vector** (round-trip `fp32→fp8→fp32` RNE when
`round_scale=1`, the heavier path measured here), instead of `2*H`
bf16 bytes. The reads are identical (keys/scores stay bf16), so
rows are directly comparable to the bf16 sections. Raw logs:
[`bristen-dsa-kpool-bench-A100-fp8.log`](bristen-dsa-kpool-bench-A100-fp8.log),
[`beverin-dsa-kpool-bench-fp8.log`](beverin-dsa-kpool-bench-fp8.log).

## Binding

Every fp8 row — like the bf16 rows — is **launch/occupancy bound**:
effective GB/s is a small fraction of the HBM roof (MI300A 5300 GB/s,
A100 2039 GB/s) and arithmetic intensity is 1.3–1.6 FLOP/B, far below
the ridge (~247 FLOP/B MI300A, ~10 FLOP/B A100). These are sub-µs
per-warp bookkeeping kernels; latency is dominated by dispatch and
single-warp occupancy, not memory or compute.

## Headline: fp8 vs bf16 (largest serving shape, ps=8)

| | A100 (bf16 → fp8) | MI300A (bf16 → fp8) |
|---|---|---|
| **PREFILL** n_pools=256 | 10.37 → 12.36 µs (**1.19x** slower) | 12.89 → 14.48 µs (**1.12x** slower) |
| **DECODE** batch=512 | 16.32 → 18.50 µs (**1.13x** slower) | 16.76 → 18.52 µs (**1.10x** slower) |

The ~10–20% per-launch cost is the **extra block-wide shared-memory
reductions** the fp8 store epilogue needs — an OR over "any element
finite" (skip gate) and a max of |mean| (the single per-vector scale)
— plus the round-trip RNE quantize. All pure compute/occupancy
overhead at one-warp-per-pool shapes; the *write* itself is half the
bf16 bytes, but the kernel was never memory-bound so the smaller store
does not buy latency. The fp8 path's value is therefore **half the
persistent cache footprint** (one byte vs two per K element, plus a
fp32 scale per vector) and **graph-capturability** (the `round_scale`
flag is a device int a prior graph node can produce on the same stream,
read on-device — never host-dereferenced).

## Method

`bench_dsa_kpool.hip` (built with `VKERNELS_BUILD_BENCHMARKS=ON`)
runs 2000 launches inside one timed `hipEvent` region, divided by
2000, over up to 40 samples (CV<5%), to beat MI300A's ~0.5 µs event
resolution and dynamic-sclk clock-domain corruption — see the bf16
[`gfx942.md`](gfx942.md) / [`A100.md`](A100.md) notes. A100 ran under
`uenv run prgenv-gnu/24.11:v1`; MI300A under system ROCm 6.3.0.

## Journal

Measured 2026-09-04 on both clusters right after landing the two A100
correctness fixes (the host-deref-of-device-pointer SIGSEGV and the
`__shfl_xor`→shared-memory reduction). Before the fixes the fp8 bench
could not run on A100 at all (segfault at first prefill launch); it now
completes clean (rc=0) on both, with the bf16 sections reproducing the
issue-60 baselines within noise. The fp8 kernels are 10–20% slower per
launch than bf16, entirely in the launch/occupancy regime — expected,
since the only added work is two shared-memory reductions and the
RNE quantize, and the kernel was never memory-bound. The trade is
deliberate: half the persistent cache footprint and a stream-correct
`round_scale` for CUDA-graph capture.

# dsa-topk — paged-MQA gated top-k logits (AMD gfx942, MI300A)

A roofline + occupancy characterization of the DSA indexer kernel in
`src/c/vkernels/kernels/dsa.{cpp,hip}` (issue #51) — the **first stage**
that feeds `dsa_sparse_fwd`: each query scores its paged KV tiles and the
integrator's top-k then selects the blocks to attend over.

$$\text{out}[b, t] = k\_scale[\,page[b,i],\,j\,] \cdot \sum_h \Big(\max\!\big(0,\, \textstyle\sum_d Q[b,h,d]\,K[page[b,i],j,d]\big) \cdot gate[b,h]\Big)$$

where `t = i*block + j`, `t < seq_lens[b]` (else left unwritten). The
host reference (`dsa_topk_logits_cpu`) is fp32 end-to-end. The device has
**two variants**, dispatched by `dsa_topk_logits_fits_lds` /
`dsa_topk_logits_fits_lds_fp8q` against gfx942's 64 KB non-optin dynamic-LDS
cap (whose opt-in ceiling EQUALS the non-optin cap — there is NO
`hipFuncSetAttribute` opt-in past 64 KB, verified on this node; see the KB
note `mi300a-dynamic-lds-no-optin`):

  * **fp32-Q** — the fast path. Q dequanted once into shared and reused
    across all H heads. Covers the GLM-5.3 `index_n_heads` (H=32,
    49,536 B < cap); the verified, byte-for-byte baseline below.
  * **fp8-Q** — the fallback for H=64..246. Q staged as **raw fp8 e4m3fnuz**
    (1 B/elem), dequanted on the fly in the dot loop with the SAME
    `fp8e4m3fnuz_to_f32` helper. The dequanted Q values, the fp32
    accumulator and the written output are **bit-identical** to the fp32-Q
    kernel, so the cross-check below (max_rel < 1e-3) carries over
    unchanged.

Measured on a CSCS beverin MI300A compute node (`srun --partition=mi300 -N1
-G1`, ROCm 6.3.0, gfx942:sramecc+:xnack-). Full raw log:
[`beverin-dsa-topk-bench.log`](beverin-dsa-topk-bench.log). Reproduce with
`meta/scripts/run_dsa_topk_bench_mi300.sh` (builds `test_dsa_topk_correct`
+ `dsa_topk_logits_bench` and runs both).

## Correctness (re-run on the bench node)

`test_dsa_topk_correct` — **PASS (0 failures)**, max_rel ≤ 1.6e-4
(threshold 1e-3) across 12 shapes: the GLM-5.3 `H=32` (fp32-Q path), the
`H=64` and `H=128` indexer multiples (fp8-Q path), `batch > 1`, and
`split_kv = 2` (perf-only, grouping-independent — verified for BOTH the
fp32-Q and fp8-Q kernels):

```
GPU: AMD Instinct MI300A (arch=gfx942:sramecc+:xnack-)
  bs=1  H=32 D=128 B=64 mt=8  nb=8  split=1  out[a=0.0625 r=0.000011]  PASS   (fp32-Q)
  bs=1  H=32 D=128 B=64 mt=16 nb=16 split=1  out[a=0.0625 r=0.000080]  PASS   (fp32-Q)
  bs=2  H=32 D=128 B=64 mt=8  nb=8  split=1  out[a=0.0625 r=0.000095]  PASS   (fp32-Q)
  bs=1  H=32 D=128 B=64 mt=8  nb=8  split=2  out[a=0.0625 r=0.000011]  PASS   (fp32-Q)
  bs=1  H=64 D=128 B=64 mt=8  nb=8  split=1  out[a=0.0938 r=0.000028]  PASS   (fp8-Q)
  bs=1  H=64 D=128 B=64 mt=16 nb=16 split=1  out[a=0.0938 r=0.000157]  PASS   (fp8-Q)
  bs=2  H=64 D=128 B=64 mt=8  nb=8  split=1  out[a=0.2500 r=0.000028]  PASS   (fp8-Q)
  bs=1  H=64 D=128 B=64 mt=8  nb=8  split=2  out[a=0.0938 r=0.000028]  PASS   (fp8-Q)

  bs=1  H=2  D=8   B=4  mt=16 nb=16 split=1  out[a=0.0020 r=0.000000]  PASS   (fp32-Q)

PASS (0 failure(s))
```

## Decode latency — GLM-5.3 indexer (the headline)

`bs=1, H=32, D=128, B=64, split=1` (the no-tuning baseline the integrator
gets by default), sweeping `max_table_len`:

| max_seq_len | mt | us(min) | us(med) |  GB/s |   AI |
|------------:|---:|--------:|--------:|------:|-----:|
|         512 |  8 |   2700  |   2703  |  0.03 | 57.2 |
|        1024 | 16 |   5376  |   5385  |  0.05 | 58.9 |
|        2048 | 32 |  10729  |  10745  |  0.07 | 59.8 |
|        4096 | 64 |  21438  |  21470  |  0.09 | 60.2 |

Latency is **linear in `max_seq_len`** (~5.25 µs/token): the grid is one
wavefront that loops over the page range sequentially. This is the "it
returns at all" baseline — the tilelang path the kernel replaces hangs at
`H ∈ {32, 64}`; this kernel is verified correct and returns in single-digit
to tens of milliseconds at decode context lengths.

## H=64 decode latency — the fp8-Q fallback (2× indexer)

The GLM-5.3 2× indexer (`H=64, D=128, B=64` stages 66,048 B as fp32-Q —
OVER the 64 KB cap, for which gfx942 has **no opt-in**; see above) runs the
fp8-Q kernel, which stages Q raw (8 KB) and dequants on the fly. Same
sweep as the headline:

| max_seq_len | mt | us(min) | us(med) |  GB/s |    AI |
|------------:|---:|--------:|--------:|------:|------:|
|         512 |  8 |   8212  |   8221  |  0.0  | 108.2 |
|        1024 | 16 |  16411  |  16419  |  0.0  | 114.4 |
|        4096 | 64 |  65590  |  65628  |  0.0  | 119.6 |

Latency is again linear in `max_seq_len` (~16.0 µs/token vs 5.24 µs/token
for H=32 — a consistent **~3.0×** per-token cost): 2× more heads (2× FMA
work per token) **and** the fp8-Q kernel re-dequants each Q element inside
the dot loop rather than once at shared load. The higher AI (108-120 vs
57-60 FLOP/byte) reflects the doubled H against the same K bytes, still
well below MI300A's ~247 ridge — i.e. the fp8-Q path trades LDS (saved:
`H*D*3` = 24 KB at H=64) for ALU (re-dequant), keeping the kernel
**occupancy-bound on the same one-wavefront grid** as H=32. `split_kv`
applies to the fp8-Q path identically (one page per split distributes the
serial page loop across CUs).

## The binding constraint is OCCUPANCY, not HBM

The roofline AI (~57-60 FLOP/byte) sits well below MI300A's ridge (~247
FLOP/byte), which on paper classifies the kernel as memory-bound. **But the
working set for these shapes is 68-560 KB — L2-resident after the 5-launch
warmup** — so the reported "GB/s" is over the L2-resident working set, NOT
a meaningful fraction of the 5300 GB/s HBM3 roof (note the 0.03-0.09 GB/s
column, i.e. ≤0.01% of HBM). The real limiter at decode is that the grid is
**one wavefront on one of MI300A's 228 CUs**; a single wavefront's serial
page loop + fp8→fp32 dequant + D=128 dot-product dependency chain bounds
the latency, not any bandwidth.

### split_kv — the critical perf knob (near-linear speedup)

`split_kv` slices the page range `[0, ceildiv(max_seq_len, B))` across more
blocks per batch (perf-only — the grouped logit is grouping-independent,
verified by `test_dsa_topk_correct` case `split=2`). At the largest decode
(`max_seq_len=4096`, one wavefront takes 21.5 ms), sweeping `split_kv` to
its maximum (`ceildiv(4096, 64) = 64` — one page per split):

| split_kv | us(min) | us(med) | GB/s | speedup |
|---------:|--------:|--------:|-----:|--------:|
|        1 |  21496  |  21523  | 0.03 |   1.0×  |
|        2 |  10761  |  10773  | 0.06 |   2.0×  |
|        4 |   5397  |   5401  | 0.13 |   4.0×  |
|        8 |   2707  |   2711  | 0.26 |   7.9×  |
|       16 |   1364  |   1366  | 0.52 |  15.8×  |
|       32 |    692  |    694  | 1.04 |  31.0×  |
|       64 |    356  |    359  | 2.08 |  59.9×  |

**Near-linear speedup to 59.9× at split=64** (the max — one page per
split, 64 of the 228 CUs used). The integrator should set

```text
split_kv = max(1, min( ceildiv(max_seq_len, block), 228 / batch_size ))
```

with `NUM_CU = 228` (MI300A / gfx942, `hipDeviceProp_t.multiProcessorCount`,
verified on this node — the `hip_capi.hpp` ABI docstring previously
stated the cap as 256). Rather than recompute it, the integrator calls the
host helper `dsa_topk_logits_split_for(batch_size, max_seq_len, block)`
(exposed through the C ABI `vk_dsa_topk_logits_split_for` and the Python
`vkernels.kernels.dsa_topk_logits_split_for`); for the headline shape it
returns 64 and the 4096-token decode drops from **21.5 ms → 0.36 ms**.

### Batch scaling is free parallelism

At `mt=8` (max_seq_len=512), `bs` scales the grid directly (one block per
batch), so latency is essentially flat as `bs` grows until the grid
approaches the CU count:

| bs | us(med) |
|---:|--------:|
|  1 |   2703  |
|  2 |   2711  |
|  4 |   2714  |
|  8 |   2714  |
| 16 |   2715  |
| 32 |   2717  |
| 64 |   2719  |

`bs` 1 → 64 (64× more work) costs **0.6% more latency** — i.e. ~64× more
queries/second at fixed latency, up to the ~228-CU ceiling after which the
grid starts serialising across waves.

## What the follow-on closes

The kernel is a scalar GEMV baseline (one lane per KV token, sequential
H-sum, K staged once per page in fp32 and reused across all H heads — no
MFMA, no tiled-key prefetch). The `dsa.hpp` docstring previously called out
a `hipFuncSetAttribute` opt-in for >64 KB LDS as follow-on #1; **that
opt-in does not exist on gfx942** (the opt-in ceiling EQUALS the non-optin
cap, 65,536 B — verified on this node; see the KB note
`mi300a-dynamic-lds-no-optin`). It is instead closed **algorithmically**:
the fp8-Q variant (`dsa_topk_logits_kernel_fp8q`, dispatched by
`dsa_topk_logits_fits_lds_fp8q`) drops Q to raw fp8 and dequants on the
fly, covering H up to 246 at D=128, B=64 (49,920 B at H=128) —
**bit-identical output** to the fp32-Q kernel, verified above.

The remaining follow-on is the one the perf numbers point at:

* **Tiled-key / MFMA-fp8 prefetch** — raises occupancy (more work per
  wavefront, fewer serial page loops) AND moves the kernel toward the
  Matrix-Core compute roof, attacking the single binding constraint
  (one wavefront on one of 228 CUs) shared by BOTH variants.

Until then, `split_kv` is the lever the integrator has — now exposed as a
single-source-of-truth host helper, `dsa_topk_logits_split_for` (C ABI
`vk_dsa_topk_logits_split_for`, Python `vkernels.kernels.dsa_topk_logits_split_for`),
so the integrator no longer hand-computes the (previously mis-stated)
`NUM_CU` formula. The numbers above are the baseline to beat.

# moe-fused — MXFP4 fused-MoE grouped GEMM (AMD gfx90a, MI250X)

An end-to-end Mixture-of-Experts layer that wires vkernels' four low-level
MXFP4 primitives into the xkernels `fused_moe_mxfp4` interface: fp4→bf16
dequantization, the gate+up grouped GEMM, SwiGLU activation, and the down
grouped GEMM with a routed scatter-add combine — fused into **two kernel
launches** (plus a tiny routing-weight gather). Weights stay in packed
MXFP4 E2M1 (2 values/byte) with ue8m0 per-group scales; no full bf16
materialization of the ~138 GB expert weight buffer.

Two tile configs are compiled in, selected by `block_size` (16 = decode,
64 = prefill). The decode config targets small-batch autoregressive decode
(BM=16, BN=64, 64 threads); the prefill config targets prompt processing
(BM=64, BN=64, 256 threads) and reuses each dequantized B tile across 64
rows instead of 16.

## Kernel (pseudocode)

```cpp
// Stage 0 — gate_up + SwiGLU (one bf16 rounding, matches xkernels oracle)
//   act[EM, ispp] = silu(clamp(A_sorted @ w13_gate + b_gate, L))
//                 · clamp(A_sorted @ w13_up   + b_up,   L)
// Stage 1 — down + routed combine (caller zero-initialises out)
//   out[M, hidden] += act @ w2^T · topk_w_sorted + b2     (atomicAdd per token)
//
// Dequant is inline in the K-loop; MFMA via the clang builtin
// __builtin_amdgcn_mfma_f32_16x16x16bf16_1k (16x16x16 tiles, K=64 per loop).
// Decode:   grid=(EM/16, N/64, 4), 64 threads; blockIdx.z splits N into 4×16.
// Prefill:  grid=(EM/64, N/64),  256 threads (4 wavefronts × 4 col fragments).
```

Full source: `src/c/vkernels/kernels/moe_fused{.hpp,.cpp,.hip}`,
`moe_device.hip` (E2M1/ue8m0 decode, bf16 rounding). The correctness oracle
is `fused_moe_mxfp4_cpu` (block-for-block mirror of the GPU path).

## What was implemented

- **Two fused kernels** (`gateup_swiglu_kernel[_prefill]`,
  `down_combine_kernel[_prefill]`): gate and up accumulate in fp32 in the
  same kernel and the SwiGLU product is rounded to bf16 once, matching the
  xkernels 2-stage oracle exactly (a split 3-kernel pipeline introduced a
  spurious intermediate bf16 rounding). SwiGLU gate is clamped to `L`
  *before* the sigmoid; up is clamped symmetrically to ±L.
- **Inline MXFP4 dequant**: E2M1 nibble → fp32 (LUT in `__constant__`),
  × ue8m0 scale (`s<<23` bit trick), → bf16, written straight to LDS. The
  gate and up weights share one LDS buffer in the prefill kernel (dequant
  gate → MFMA → dequant up → MFMA) to cap LDS at 16 KB.
- **Flat-index `sorted_ids`**: `moe_align_block_size` stores
  `token*top_k + sel` (padded with `M*top_k`), so the routing-weight gather
  keeps the selection index for `top_k > 1`; `act_scratch` is indexed by
  sorted row (not token), so a token routed to multiple experts never races.
- **MFMA fragment layout** (verified empirically with one-hot matrices):
  A `m=lane%16`, B `n=lane%16`, C `col=lane%16, row=(lane/16)*4+i`
  (4 consecutive rows × 1 column per lane).
- **Prefill tile config**: BM=64/BN=64/BK=64, 256 threads, 4 column
  fragments per wavefront. Added in a follow-up for the M>32 regime; the
  BN was later narrowed 128→64 to lift occupancy (see Caveats).
- **Double-buffering experiment** (documented in Caveats): 2-stage LDS was
  implemented, measured, and **reverted** — it halved decode occupancy and
  cost ~50%.

## Workload

- **Device**: AMD Instinct **MI250X** (2 GCDs; benchmarks run on device 0 =
  one GCD, ~110 CU). gfx90a, ROCm 6.2.4. Measured on the beverin `mi200`
  partition inside the `vkernels:hip-full` container (image 20.8 GB, loaded
  per job from `/capstor/scratch/cscs/xyao/vkernels-full-v2.tar`).
- **Config**: E=256 experts, hidden=4096, ispp=512, top_k=6, group_size=32,
  SwiGLU clamp L=10. Random routing. Weights are random MXFP4 (E2M1) with
  unit (127) ue8m0 scales, zero biases.
- **Baseline**: xkernels' reference torch loop
  (`bench_xkernels_torch.py`) — per-expert `dequant_mxfp4_weight` →
  `A[t] @ w13e.T` → SiLU → `act @ w2e.T` → `index_add_`, in torch (no
  Triton; the Triton backend segfaults under ROCm 6.2.4 on both gfx90a and
  gfx942). Exact-match-verified against the vkernels CPU oracle.
- **Correctness**: GPU output matches the CPU oracle to
  `max_rel < 0.00001` (decode) and `< 0.02` (prefill).

**Reproduce** (on a gfx90a host with the image loaded):

```bash
podman run --rm --device=/dev/kfd --device=/dev/dri --security-opt seccomp=unconfined \
  -v /users/xyao/vkernels-prefill:/workspace/vkernels vkernels:hip-full \
  /workspace/vkernels/build-hip-prefill/meta/benchmarks/moe_fused_bench
# and: .../moe_fused_prefill_bench , .../moe_bench , .../test_moe_fused_correct
```

## Results — decode regime (E=256, hidden=4096, ispp=512, top_k=6)

Latency is the median of 10 iterations (3 warmups), HIP-event timed. `EM`
is the padded sorted-row count. **GFLOP/s = 6·M·ispp·hidden·top_k / t**
(2·MAC × the gate+up+down GEMMs × the top_k routed experts — the *useful*
arithmetic; padded EM rows are extra work not counted).

| M | EM | vkernels (ms) | xkernels torch (ms) | speedup | GFLOP/s | note |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---|
| 1  | 96   | 0.648 | 6.0 | 9.3× | 117 | 96 padded rows vs 6 real |
| 2  | 192  | 0.821 | — | — | 184 | |
| 4  | 384  | 1.189 | — | — | 254 | |
| 8  | 768  | 3.446 | ~30 | ~8.7× | 175 | |
| 16 | 1408 | 3.983 | ~40 | ~10× | 303 | |
| 32 | 2432 | 9.029 | — | — | 268 | |
| 48 | 3456 | 10.326 | 162.2 | 15.7× | 351 | 3456 padded vs 288 real (12× waste) |

The decode regime is padding-dominated: per-expert 16-row blocks mean EM
scales with the number of *routed experts*, not tokens, so effective
throughput stays at ~0.1% of the ~191 TFLOP/s per-GCD bf16 roof.

## Results — prefill vs decode (E=8, hidden=4096, ispp=512, top_k=2)

Dense routing (E=8, so each 64-row block fills once M ≥ 512). GFLOP/s =
6·M·ispp·hidden·top_k / t.

| M | decode (ms) | decode GFLOP/s | prefill (ms) | prefill GFLOP/s | speedup |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 128  | 0.958 | 3364 | 1.175 | 2740 | 0.81× |
| 256  | 1.356 | 4752 | 1.201 | 5365 | 1.13× |
| 512  | 2.697 | 4777 | 1.945 | 6625 | 1.39× |
| 1024 | 5.151 | 5003 | 2.993 | 8609 | 1.72× |
| 2048 | 10.236 | 5035 | 5.781 | 8916 | 1.77× |

The prefill config (BN=64) wins from M ≥ 256; below that the 64-row padding
waste dominates and decode is faster. Peak prefill throughput is ~8.9
TFLOP/s ≈ 4.7% of the ~191 TFLOP/s per-GCD roof — the kernel is
occupancy-bound (see Caveats).

## Results — primitives (microbenchmarks)

Single-wavefront microbenchmarks of the four low-level building blocks
(`bench_moe.hip`); the MFMA number is a **dependent-chain floor** (one
accumulator, `__asm__ __volatile__`), not a throughput ceiling.

| Primitive | Result | Roof / note |
|---|---|---|
| K16 MFMA (16×16×16bf16) | 0.431 TFLOP/s | dependent chain, 1 wavefront; not the device roof |
| K32 emulation (2×K16) | 0.363 TFLOP/s | 84% of K16 (amortizes the loop) |
| fp4→bf16 dequant | 279 GElem/s | 537M elems, scalar LUT path |
| LDS fill (global_load_dwordx4) | 4898 GB/s | 64 threads × uint4, exceeds HBM roof (LDS-bound) |

## Caveats and notes

- **One GCD, not the full package.** MI250X exposes 2 GCDs; every number
  above is device 0 alone (one GCD ≈ 110 CU ≈ 191 TFLOP/s bf16). The bench's
  printed "383 TFLOP/s" roof is the whole 2-GCD package. A real deployment
  would shard experts across both GCDs (~2×).
- **Occupancy-bound, not barrier-bound.** LDS double-buffering (2-stage
  sA/sB) was implemented and reverted: it doubled decode LDS 6→12 KB,
  halving blocks/CU, and slowed decode ~50% (e.g. 1.43→2.11 ms at M=256).
  The redundant barrier between the A-tile load and the weight dequant was
  removed (they write different LDS buffers) — a free, small win. Acting on
  this, the prefill BN was narrowed 128→64 (24→16 KB LDS, 64→32 accumulator
  VGPRs), lifting occupancy 2→3 blocks/CU for a measured ~1.5× (M=2048:
  8.75→5.78 ms). The lever is *more* occupancy, not deeper pipelining.
- **~1.5% of peak, and it's the dequant, not the MFMA.** Each block
  dequantizes every fp4 weight inline (LUT + scale + bf16 convert), which is
  ALU-heavy relative to the 16×16×16 MFMAs it feeds. Materializing weights
  once (xkernels Triton's approach) trades 138 GB of HBM traffic for this
  ALU; the fused kernel wins by never touching that buffer.
- **Decode padding waste.** `moe_align_block_size` pads every routed expert
  to a 16-row block, so small-M latency is ~(experts routed)·16 rows, not
  M tokens. A padding-aware launch (skip empty block tails) would help M<32.
- **gfx90a constraints.** >64-thread blocks crash with hand-pinned VGPRs;
  `__volatile__` on MFMA asm breaks accumulation; `reinterpret_cast` on
  `void*` is rejected in device code (C-style casts required). The fused
  kernel sidesteps all three (builtin MFMA, 64-thread decode blocks, C
  casts).
- **Baseline is torch, not Triton.** xkernels' Triton backend segfaults
  under ROCm 6.2.4 on both gfx90a and gfx942 (SIGSEGV inside Triton 3.3.1),
  so the comparison is against the reference torch loop.

## Journal

**What was done.** Wired the four MXFP4 primitives (issues #12–15) into a
2-launch fused MoE matching xkernels' `fused_moe_mxfp4` interface, with a
CPU oracle, Python bindings, and a prefill (BM=64/BN=64) tile config.
Benchmarked on MI250X and recorded under `docs/performance/`.

**Challenges.**
1. *Fragment layout.* The MFMA C fragment is 4 consecutive rows × 1 column
   per lane (not a 4×4 sub-tile) — pinned down empirically with one-hot
   matrices before the kernel could be correct.
2. *Single bf16 rounding.* A 3-kernel split (gate, up, combine) rounds the
   activation twice and mismatches the oracle; gate+up must share one kernel
   so `silu(g)·u` is rounded once.
3. *Register pinning vs. reliability.* Hand-pinned VGPR asm crashed for
   >64-thread blocks and broke accumulation with `__volatile__`; the fused
   kernel uses the clang builtin, which keeps register allocation correct
   across ROCm versions.
4. *Double-buffering didn't pay.* The occupancy loss (6→12 KB LDS) outweighed
   the load→MFMA overlap; reverted after measurement (see Caveats).
5. *Occupancy was the real lever.* Narrowing the prefill BN 128→64 (same
   64-row M-tile, half the columns) traded B-tile reuse for occupancy
   (2→3 blocks/CU) and won ~1.5× across the board — the dequant ALU is the
   bottleneck, and more resident warps hide it better than wider tiles reuse it.

**Future work.**
- Shard across both MI250X GCDs and measure the ~2× scaling.
- Raise occupancy further: a BM=32 prefill tile (or `__launch_bounds__`
  nudging) could cut VGPRs below 64 and reach 4 blocks/CU; split gate/up to
  reduce live registers is another path.
- Wavefront-specialised producer/consumer dequant once occupancy saturates.
- Revisit the Triton baseline when ROCm 6.3 / a fixed Triton ships.

  halving blocks/CU, and slowed decode ~50% on gfx90a. The redundant barrier
  between the A-tile load and the weight dequant was removed (they write
  different LDS buffers) — a free, small win. Acting on this, the prefill BN
  was narrowed 128→64 (24→16 KB LDS, 64→32 accumulator VGPRs), lifting
  occupancy 2→3 blocks/CU and measuring ~1.3–1.8× faster on gfx942 (M=2048:
  2.58→1.98 ms). The lever is *more* occupancy, not deeper pipelining.
- **~1.5% of peak, and it's the dequant, not the MFMA.** Each block
  dequantizes every fp4 weight inline (LUT + scale + bf16 convert), which is
  ALU-heavy relative to the 16×16×16 MFMAs it feeds. Materializing weights
  once (xkernels Triton's approach) trades 138 GB of HBM traffic for this
  ALU; the fused kernel wins by never touching that buffer.
- **Decode padding waste.** `moe_align_block_size` pads every routed expert
  to a 16-row block, so small-M latency is ~(experts routed)·16 rows, not
  M tokens. A padding-aware launch (skip empty block tails) would help M<32.
- **MI300A decode timing is noisy across nodes.** The APU clock throttles
  with sustained load, so decode M=2048 has been seen anywhere from 3.6 to
  5.0 ms on different `mi300` nodes. The prefill-vs-decode speedups above are
  measured within a single run (same node, same clock state) and are the
  trustworthy comparison; absolute latencies carry ~±30% across nodes.
- **Baseline is torch, not Triton.** xkernels' Triton backend segfaults
  under ROCm 6.2.4 on both gfx90a and gfx942 (SIGSEGV inside Triton 3.3.1),
  so the comparison is against the reference torch loop.
- **SLURM note.** The container image is not shared across compute nodes:
  each `mi300` job must `podman load` it into a fresh `--root/--runroot`
  (in `/tmp`, not the stale `/dev/shm` default), then mount
  `/users/xyao/vkernels-prefill` at `/workspace/vkernels`.

## CPU oracle — host validation surface (issue #41)

Acceptance criterion #1 requires the gfx942 kernel to be "validated against
the CPU oracle at K3 shapes (E=256, hidden=7168, ispp=33792, top_k=16)."
The HIP bench carries a `--no-cpu` flag that skips that check for exactly
the reason called out above ("~1.5% of peak, and it's the dequant" and
"Decode padding waste"): at K3 *decode* (M=1, top_k=16) `moe_align_block_size`
pads each routed expert to a 16-row block, so EM=256 rows hold only 16 real
rows — **93.8% of the oracle's GEMM is over padding rows whose A tile is
zero and which contribute exactly zero.** The CPU reference therefore spends
most of its time on provably-zero work, which is what made the per-call check
impractical to run inside a sweep.

Two bit-exact optimizations to the CPU reference (`src/c/vkernels/kernels/moe_fused.cpp`)
make K3-routing validation feasible on the host:

1. **Padding-skip GEMM.** `moe_gateup_cpu`/`moe_down_cpu` now `continue` past
   rows with `sorted_ids[...] >= N` in the gate/up/down dot-product loops.
   Padding rows already hold the zeroed-tile result (the accumulator is
   zeroed per N-block), so skipping their dot products changes zero output
   bits.  At M=1 this removes ~15/16 of the GEMM.
2. **LUT dequant + per-group scale hoist.** `dequant_weight_tile` reads the
   16-entry fp4-nibble decode and the 256-entry ue8m0 scale from tables
   built once from `fp4nib_to_f32bits_local`/`ue8m0_to_float` (bit-identical
   by construction) instead of re-running the branchy decode twice per
   packed byte, and hoists the per-group ue8m0 scale (shared across
   `group_size` K elements) out of the per-byte loop.  The original loop is
   kept as the golden `dequant_weight_tile_ref`.

**Verification.** A new host-only bench, `meta/benchmarks/bench_moe_fused_oracle.cpp`
(the always-runnable analog of `bench_rccl.cpp`/`bench_pipeline_boundary.cpp`,
no GPU/ROCm), times the reference at the K3 decode routing shape.  Same
`-O3` build, M=1 / top_k=16 / E=256 (93.8% padding):

| shape (M hidden ispp) | before µs | after µs | speedup |
|-----------------------|----------:|---------:|--------:|
| 1  512  1024          |   303 305 |   66 414 |  4.57×  |
| 2  512  1024          |   606 548 |  151 633 |  4.00×  |
| 4  512  1024          |   969 772 |  261 280 |  3.71×  |
| 1  7168  128          |   461 764 |  125 599 |  3.68×  |

The speedup shrinks as M grows (92.7% at M=4, 90.4% at M=8) — exactly the
expected shape of a padding-skip win.

Bit-exactness is asserted, not assumed: `tests/kernels/moe/test_moe_fused.cpp`
adds `Fp4DequantLUTBitExact` (every one of the 256×256 packed-byte × ue8m0-
scale pairs via `memcmp`) and `Fp4DequantLUTHoistVaryingScale` (300 random
tiles with scale varying across the two K-groups, exercising the hoist).
`K3RoutingTopK16` runs the full oracle at E=256 / top_k=16 / M=1 and checks
both the act map (real rows = `SwiGLU(hidden)`, padding rows = 0) and the
combined output (`top_k · act · ispp`) against analytically-known values —
so the GPU kernel has a correct, fast reference to match at the K3 routing
shape the issue names.

**Scope.** Full-K3 hidden/ispp (7168 × 33792) validation stays host-memory-
bound (~6 TB of expert weights cannot be held on a normal host); the
realistic surface is K3 *routing* (top_k=16, E=256, M=1) at a moderate
hidden/ispp where the weights fit.  The routing, block alignment and
`top_k=16` combine paths are identical at either scale — this is the part
the bench and the new tests cover, and the part the GPU-side work
(items 1–5) actually changes.

**On-hardware validation (beverin, MI300A / gfx942, job 599347).**  The
host oracle bench and the GPU bench were built with the `hip` preset
(gfx942, `VKERNELS_BUILD_BENCHMARKS=ON`) on a compute node and run on the
MI300A.  The GPU kernel is **validated against the optimized CPU oracle
at the K3 routing shape (E=256, hidden=7168, top_k=16, `--kmajor`)** with
`cpu-rel < 0.03` and `status = ok` for every M — acceptance criterion #1,
now runnable end-to-end on real hardware because the oracle is fast enough:

| M | EM | evt µs | bch µs | TFLOP/s | cpu-rel | status |
|---|---:|-------:|-------:|--------:|--------:|--------|
| 1 |  256 | 1107.7 | 1103.0 | 0.020 | 0.00157 | ok |
| 2 |  512 | 1250.8 | 1244.6 | 0.035 | 0.029   | ok |
| 4 | 1024 | 1824.1 | 1817.3 | 0.048 | 0.0292  | ok |

For reference, the host oracle bench on the same node's CPUs measures
39.3 ms (E=256 h512 i1024 k16 M=1) and 67.2 ms (E=256 h7168 i128 k16 M=1).

**On-hardware A/B of the dequant (the dominant oracle cost), same MI300A
node, bit-exact.**  `bench_dequant_ab` times
`dequant_weight_tile` (optimized: LUT nibble/scale decode + per-group
ue8m0 scale hoisting) vs `dequant_weight_tile_ref` (the original per-byte
loop) over the exact tile grid the oracle walks for one real expert's
gate+up weights, after re-asserting the two are bit-identical on the
bench's own data.  This is the reproducible before/after for the changed
function (the earlier full-oracle 4.6× was measured on a different
development host and its log was not preserved, so it is no longer cited).

| shape | tiles/expert | ref µs/tile | opt µs/tile | speedup | bit-exact |
|-------|-------------:|------------:|------------:|--------:|-----------|
| h7168 i512  (K3) | 1792 | 15.24 | 5.40 | **2.82×** | 7 340 032 vals |
| h7168 i128       |  448 | 15.21 | 5.35 | **2.84×** | 1 835 008 vals |
| h4096 i512 (def) | 1024 | 15.22 | 5.39 | **2.82×** | 4 194 304 vals |

The ratio is stable (~2.8×) across shapes, so the oracle — whose time is
dominated by the real-expert dequant — sees ~2.8× on this hardware.
Full log: `docs/performance/moe-fused/beverin-dequant-ab.log`.

The full-K3 decode shape (ispp=33792, `--dummy --no-cpu`) does **not**
run on the current single-GPU kernel, for two reasons found on beverin:

1. **`int` buffer-size overflow in `bench_moe_fused.hip` (fixed).**  The
   bench computed `w13_sz = E*2*ispp*(hidden/2)` etc. in `int`; at K3 shapes
   this exceeds `INT_MAX` (e.g. 61.9 GB), wraps negative, and as `size_t`
   threw `std::length_error` (real weights) or a spurious
   `hipMalloc("w13s"): out of memory` (`--dummy`).  The earlier "does not
   fit" note was partly this artifact.  Fixed by computing the four `_sz`
   constants in `size_t` (`static_cast<std::size_t>(E) * ...`), mirroring the
   casts in the CPU oracle / tests.  After the fix, ispp=1024 and 2048 run
   cleanly; the K3 *routing* latency-vs-ispp (per-GPU-relevant shape) is:

   | ispp | M=1 µs | M=2 µs | M=4 µs | M=8 µs |
   |-----:|-------:|-------:|-------:|-------:|
   |  512 |   825  |  1058  |  1697  |   —    | (CPU oracle: all ok)
   | 1024 |  1289  |  1896  |  3659  |  7389  |
   | 2048 |  2249  |  3980  |  7916  |   —    |

   (`--kmajor`, gfx942; full numbers in
   `docs/performance/moe-fused/beverin-k3-scaling.txt`.)  The default harness
   (E=256 h4096 i512 k6, swiglu) measures M=1 = 398 µs — matching the
   issue's "~0.45 ms" baseline for acceptance criterion #2.

2. **GPU memory-access fault at ispp ≥ 4096 (and at full K3 ispp=33792, any
   E), `--kmajor`-independent.**  Even with the size fix and only ~12 GB
   resident (E=32, the per-GPU TP=8 shard), the kernel faults: `Memory
   access fault by GPU node-4 ... Reason: Unknown` — and it faults identically
   with and without `--kmajor` (item 4's K-major repack), so it is not the
   K-major path; it is a deeper internal index/stride assumption at large
   ispp.  This is a pre-existing kernel limitation, **not** the oracle work,
   and is worth investigating separately: the issue reports K3 serving
   *works* (6/6 factual probes), so the vLLM invocation likely differs from
   this single-GPU bench shape (tile sizes, the act/weight strides, or a
   different kernel variant).  Until that is reconciled, the bench cannot
   produce the full-K3 (ispp=33792) single-decode latency; the
   moderate-ispp routing numbers above and the default-harness 398 µs are
   the validated per-GPU baselines for acceptance criterion #2
   (~0.45 ms → ≤ 0.30 ms).  Item 5 (wavefront-specialised dequant) is the
   remaining GPU lever toward that target.

## Journal

**What was done.** Validated the fused MoE (decode + prefill) and the four
primitives on MI300A (gfx942) after the gfx90a bring-up, and recorded the
results under `docs/performance/`. Prefill correctness passes at
`max_rel < 0.02`, decode at `max_rel < 0.00001`.

**Challenges.**
1. *Cross-node image loading.* SLURM jobs land on different MI300A nodes,
   none of which share the login node's podman storage. The working recipe
   is a fresh per-job `podman --root $PR/root --runroot $PR/run load` into
   `/tmp` (the default `/dev/shm` root carries a stale boot-ID after node
   reboots and fails with exit 125).
2. *Triton baseline unavailable.* xkernels' Triton backend SIGSEGVs under
   ROCm 6.2.4 + Triton 3.3.1 on both architectures, so the baseline is the
   torch loop (which gfx942 also accelerates ~1.3× over gfx90a).
3. *Occupancy was the real lever.* Narrowing the prefill BN 128→64 (24→16 KB
   LDS, 64→32 accumulator VGPRs) lifted occupancy 2→3 blocks/CU and won
   ~1.3–1.8× on gfx942, consistent with the ~1.5× measured cleanly on gfx90a.

**Future work.**
- Raise occupancy further: a BM=32 prefill tile (or `__launch_bounds__`
  nudging) could cut VGPRs below 64 and reach 4 blocks/CU; split gate/up to
  reduce live registers is another path.
- Wavefront-specialised producer/consumer dequant once occupancy saturates.
- Revisit the Triton baseline when ROCm 6.3 / a fixed Triton ships.
